pages.title: Introduction
pages.blurb: What Wildcard Pipeline is and how the pieces fit.

sections.title: What does it do?
sections.text:
Each time you press Generate, Wildcard Pipeline picks from your lists, follows your rules and fills in your prompt. You get a different prompt every run without typing.
For example: a wildcard called "subject" holds a cat, a dog and a fox. Your template says A photo of $subject. Each run picks one animal and writes the prompt.

sections.title: How the pieces fit together
sections.text:
You wire three nodes in ComfyUI:
- WP Context holds your modules (wildcards, fixed values, combines and so on) and turns them into $variables every run.
- WP Prompt Assembler fills your template with those variables.
- CLIP Text Encode, the normal ComfyUI node, takes the prompt to your sampler.
Figure: Modules run in the WP Context, which passes $variables to the Assembler, which passes the prompt to CLIP. Diagram of the pipeline. Across the top, labelled modules inside the Context, sit five module kinds: Wildcard, Fixed Values, Combine, Derivation and Constraint, with a down arrow into the flow below. The flow runs left to right: WP Context (rolls + resolves), an arrow labelled emits, a group of resolved $vars chips ($subject, $style, $lighting), an arrow labelled fills, Prompt Assembler (with a template beginning 'A $style portrait…'), an arrow labelled prompt, and CLIP Encode (conditioning). Caption: modules resolve inside WP Context into named $variables, which go to the WP Prompt Assembler and then to CLIP.

sections.title: What are modules?
sections.text:
Modules are the pieces you build in this manager. Each one sets or changes $variables:
- Wildcard: a list of options; one is picked each run.
- Fixed Values: text that stays the same.
- Combine: builds one phrase from several variables.
- Derivation: if/then rules that change variables based on what was picked.
- Constraint: makes some options of a later wildcard likelier or rule them out, based on an earlier pick.
Make and edit modules here in the manager, then add them to a WP Context on the canvas.

sections.title: A finished graph
sections.text: Figure: The whole pipeline: a WP Context holding the Starter set bundle, then WP Prompt Assembler, CLIP Text Encode and KSampler. Screenshot of four nodes left to right on the ComfyUI canvas. A WP Context (seed 42, fixed, modules 6 / 6) holds the Starter set bundle, expanded to show Starter subject (wildcard), Starter pairing (constraint, #1-all), Starter mood (wildcard, #1), Starter style (fixed), Starter scene (combine) and Starter accent (derivation). Its context output feeds a WP Prompt Assembler with the template '$scene, $style, $accent, masterpiece, highly detailed', chips $style, $scene and $accent, and the resolved preview 'sleepy wolf, oil painting, soft lighting, masterpiece, highly detailed'. The prompt output goes into CLIP Text Encode (Prompt), whose CONDITIONING goes into the positive input of a KSampler. It shows the whole pipeline: modules in a Context, a template in the Assembler, then the usual ComfyUI nodes.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
Try right-clicking. Most WP nodes, and the rows inside them, have a menu: save a row to the library, pull in a library change, duplicate, and more.
Finding your way in these docs: / jumps to the search box, which searches the text of every page and opens a result at its section (Enter opens the first). On a wide window, On this page on the right lists a page's sections; hover a section title for a link to it. Click a screenshot to see it full size, and use Previous and Next at the foot of a page to read on.

pages.title: Quick start
pages.blurb: Build the smallest working pipeline in a few minutes.

sections.title: Step 1: Make a wildcard
sections.text:
Click the button below. The wildcard editor opens with a "subject" wildcard filled in: a cat, a dog and a fox, all equally likely. Change the options if you like, then click Save.
Figure: The New wildcard form filled in by the button: a subject wildcard with a cat, a dog and a fox. Nothing is saved until you press Save. Screenshot of the whole New wildcard page in the manager (breadcrumb Library › Wildcards › New wildcard) after pressing Create a starter wildcard. Identity: Name 'subject', Category None, Variable name $subject, an empty Description, Tags with an Add button, and Content rating with a Mark as NSFW (18+) switch. Sub-categories says No sub-categories yet. Options (3) lists 'a cat', 'a dog' and 'a fox', each with weight 1, sub-category (none), a + negative button and a 33% probability bar; above the table are Bulk edit, Add null and Add option. Cancel and Save sit at the bottom right; nothing is stored until you press Save.

sections.title: Step 2: Wire it up in ComfyUI
sections.text:
On the ComfyUI canvas:
- Add a WP Context. Double-click the canvas and search "WP Context", or right-click → Add Node → wildcard-pipeline → WP Context.
- Add your wildcard to the context. Click Add module on the WP Context and pick the "subject" wildcard you just saved.
- Add a WP Prompt Assembler and wire the Context's context output into it. Type the template A photo of $subject.
- Wire the Assembler's prompt into your CLIP Text Encode's text input.
- Generate. Each run picks a subject and writes the prompt.
Figure: The finished chain: a WP Context with one wildcard, a WP Prompt Assembler ('A photo of $subject'), CLIP Text Encode and KSampler. Screenshot of the quick start chain on the canvas, four nodes left to right. A WP Context (seed 42, fixed, modules 1 / 1) holds one wildcard row, Starter subject ('$subject · 4 options'). Its context feeds a WP Prompt Assembler with the template 'A photo of $subject', one $subject chip and the preview 'A photo of wolf'. The prompt output goes into the text input of CLIP Text Encode (Prompt), and its CONDITIONING goes into the positive input of a KSampler (steps 20, cfg 8.0, euler, simple). Each Generate rolls a new subject through the same chain.

sections.title: Step 3: See what was picked
sections.text: Wire a WP Debug to the Context's context output to see what $subject picked on each run.

sections.title: What to try next
sections.text: Add more modules: a Fixed Values for a style that stays the same, a Combine to join two variables, or a Constraint so two picks agree. A WP Context Loop makes several variations in one Generate.

pages.title: Test Runner
pages.blurb: Run modules on many seeds, inspect each one, and compare against a baseline.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
The Test Runner, in the manager sidebar, runs a stack of your library modules through the real engine, once per seed, and shows what comes out. Use it to check that a wildcard's options all come up, that a constraint actually fires, or that a combine reads the variables you think it does, before you wire anything on the canvas.
Figure: An empty Test Runner: saved scenarios on the left, the stack and pinned values in the middle, and Range / Random seeds with Run at the top. Screenshot of the manager's Test Runner page. On the left, Scenarios with a New button, a filter box and an unsaved Quick run ('No saved scenarios yet. Build a stack, run it, then Save to keep it here.'). In the middle, Quick run (0 items · seeds 0 to 99) with Range / Random, from 0 and 100 seeds, Save scenario and Run at the top; a Stack section ('runs left to right, like the modules on a Context node') with Add module or bundle; and Pinned values ('stand in for a value an upstream node would pass in') with Pin a value.
Figure: A seed here is a real chain seed: the same seed on a canvas Context holding the same modules gives the same values. Steps: Scenario (stack + pins + seeds) → ctrl + enter → Run (real engine, seeded) → per seed → Results (values, traces, warnings) → save → Baseline (compare after edits). Flow diagram of four stages left to right: Scenario (stack + pins + seeds), an arrow labelled Ctrl + Enter, Run (real engine, seeded), an arrow labelled per seed, Results (values, traces, warnings), an arrow labelled save, and Baseline (compare after edits). Caption: a seed here is a real chain seed, so the same seed on a canvas Context holding the same modules gives the same values.

sections.title: Build a scenario
sections.text:
A scenario is what one Context node would hold, saved so you can run it again. Press New in the rail, then Add module or bundle. Cards run left to right, like the modules on a Context; drag them (or Alt + arrow keys) to reorder, and use a card's switch to leave it out of a run without removing it.
Stack
The modules and bundles to run, in order. A card warns when it reads a $variable nothing earlier sets, or when a combine template is plain text and will never vary.
Pinned values
Stand-ins for what a node further up the graph would pass in, such as $subject from an Injector. They are set before the first card runs.
Seeds
Range runs seeds from N upward; Random draws a fresh set each run. Up to 10,000 seeds per run.
Output
The variable treated as the prompt: the last combine's output unless you pick another on the Outputs tab.
Save (Ctrl+S) keeps the scenario, and the pin icon keeps it at the top of the rail. From a module or bundle editor, Send to Test Runner opens a quick run with just that item, and In N scenarios lists the saved scenarios that use it.

sections.title: Read a run
sections.text:
The stats row gives runs, unique outputs, warnings and engine time. Below it, each tab answers one question:
Variables
Every $variable and how often it took each value, with values that never changed listed once as constants.
Outputs
The output for the first seeds, tinted by which variable wrote each part, with a NEG line for the negative words it carries.
Samples
One row per seed with every variable (and the output's negative, when there is one); filter by seed or value.
Warnings
Runtime warnings grouped by kind, with the seeds that raised them, and any runs that failed.
Compare
What changed since the saved baseline. See below.
Click any seed to open its trace: every card in run order with what it wrote, plus the nested @{…} picks it made on the way. Copy seed puts it on the clipboard for a canvas Context.

sections.title: Inspect a module
sections.text:
Click a stack card to open its inspector: how that module is set up next to what the last run did with it.
Wildcard
Each option's share of the weight next to its share of the picks. Options that were never picked are flagged; picks through @{} references elsewhere in the stack count too.
Constraint
Which pick it listens to, which wildcard it re-weights and how far it reaches, and how many times it applied. Zero usually means the target runs before the source.
Combine
The template, the $variables it reads, and the outputs it produced.
Derivation
Its rules as plain if / else lines, and the values its target ended up with.
Fixed values
Every name and value it sets.
Bundle
Its modules in run order (nested bundles indented) and the values each one wrote.
Edit in the inspector opens that module in its editor.

sections.title: Baselines: catch what an edit changed
sections.text:
On the Compare tab of a saved scenario, Save as baseline keeps this run's output for each seed (the first 1,000), plus every variable's spread and the warnings. Edit your modules, run again, and the tab lists each seed whose output changed (with the changed words marked), values that appeared or disappeared, shares that moved, and warnings that came or went. A seed whose negative changed is listed too; a baseline saved before negatives existed says negative not recorded until you save it again.
Re-run all in the rail's Pinned header runs every pinned scenario against its baseline in one go, and each row then reads matches or N changed. When the result is the new normal, Use this run as baseline replaces it.
Compare needs the same seeds on both sides. A Range scenario always has them; for a Random one, Run the baseline's seeds reruns exactly the seeds the baseline used.

pages.title: Library health
pages.blurb: Check the whole library: broken references, likely mistakes, unused items, and how varied each bundle is.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
After a few months of imports, AI packs and deletes, a library collects references to wildcards that are gone, constraint rules for options that were renamed, near-duplicates and items nothing uses. The canvas warnings only look at one chain. Library health, in the manager sidebar under Library, looks at everything at once.
Figure: Library health: the three counts at the top, the filter and search, and one fold-out list per check, each row with Open and Ignore. Screenshot of the Library health page. At the top, three cards count 4 problems (print wrong or nothing), 3 warnings (probably a mistake) and 5 to tidy up, above a filter (All, Problems, Warnings, Tidy up) and a search box. Below, one fold-out list per check: Points at a wildcard that's gone lists the Fantasy hero bundle and the Outfit wildcard, which point at a deleted Shoes wildcard; Constraint rule for an option or tag that's gone lists Class → Weapon with two rules for "heavy" and "warrior"; Reads a variable nothing sets lists the Scene combine reading $pose; Wildcards with the same options lists Mood (2) with a link to Mood. Each row has Open and Ignore.
The sidebar entry shows a red count when there are problems and an amber one when there are only warnings, and the Dashboard shows the same counts with the first problem. The page checks again on its own a moment after you change the library; Check again runs it now.

sections.title: Problems: print wrong or nothing
sections.text:
Points at a wildcard that’s gone
A @{reference} in an option, combine, fixed value, derivation, saved template or bundle copy names a wildcard no longer in the library. It prints nothing where it sits.
Constraint lost its wildcard
Its source or target wildcard was deleted, so it never applies.
Constraint rule for an option or tag that’s gone
A matrix tag or an exception value the wildcard no longer has. That rule never matches.
Bundle holds a bundle that’s gone
A nested bundle was deleted, so inserting the outer one skips it.
Empty bundle
Inserting it adds nothing.
Wildcard can’t pick anything
No options, only the empty option, or every option at weight 0 with no fallback.
Reads a variable nothing sets
A $variable no library item, WP Model Info, WP Context Loop or the open canvas sets. Unless a WP Context Injector sets it, it prints as empty.

sections.title: Warnings: probably a mistake
sections.text:
No name
Hard to find in pickers and references.
Same name twice
Two items of one kind with one name. The row links to both.
Wildcards with the same options
Often a pack imported twice.
Same option listed twice
It rolls twice as often. Raise one option’s weight instead.
Options that never roll
Weight 0 and not the fallback.
Two wildcards write the same variable
On one chain the later one wins, which is fine when they are alternatives.
Bundle copies of deleted items
The bundle still runs its copies, but they no longer follow the library. Open the bundle to relink them.

sections.title: Tidy up: clutter
sections.text:
Not used by any bundle, template or reference
Nothing in the library uses it, and it is not on the open canvas. Delete all removes every one shown, after one confirm.
Sets a variable nothing in the library reads
A combine, derivation or fixed value whose variable no saved template, combine, derivation or open Assembler prints.
Bundle holds an older copy
The library item changed since the bundle was saved.
Tag used only once
With a hint when it looks like a typo of another tag (outfit / outfits).
Empty category
Nothing is filed under it. Delete removes the category only.
Newer version on Community
The author published a newer version of a pack you installed. Update opens the same dialog as the list pages.
Installed from a newer format
It came from a newer Wildcard Pipeline, so settings this version doesn’t know were left out. Update the extension and reinstall it.

sections.title: Open your canvas first
sections.text:
A WP Context keeps its own copy of what you insert, so the library can't tell what sits on a canvas. When a ComfyUI tab is open, the page asks it which library items it holds, which variables its Injectors, Loops and Model Info set, and which $variables its Assemblers read, and counts those as used. Ids and names only, never values.
With no canvas open, the page says so: items you only use on a canvas show under Not used. Open your workflow in another tab and press Check again, or Ignore them.

sections.title: Fix, ignore, filter
sections.text:
Open
Opens the item’s editor (a tag opens the items carrying it). Rows about two items, like duplicates, link to each one.
Delete
Only on rows where it is safe: unused items and empty categories. Copies on a canvas keep working, and a backup from Settings › Library & data can bring an item back.
Ignore
Hides the row for good and leaves it out of the counts. Show ignored brings ignored rows back so you can Unignore them. If the same item turns up for a different reason, it shows again.
Filter and search
All, Problems, Warnings or Tidy up, and a search over item names, details and values.

sections.title: Variety check
sections.text: Under the findings, every bundle has Check variety. It runs the bundle 200 times with random seeds through the real engine and shows how many of the results were different, which variables never changed although their wildcard has more options, which options never came up, and the run's warnings. Open in Test Runner takes the same bundle to the Test Runner for a closer look.

pages.title: Themes and looks
pages.blurb: Pick the manager's colours and its look separately, and mix any of them.

sections.title: Colours
sections.text:
- Orbit: Logo indigo on cool ink. The default.
- Native: ComfyUI's own greys.
- Nebula: Violet-tinted night with a violet accent.
- Tide: Deep slate blue with a sky accent.
- Ember: Warm charcoal and paper with a copper accent.
- High contrast: Black and white, solid borders, a yellow focus ring.
Module kind colours (wildcard, fixed value, combine and the rest), variable colours and the teal of a picked option stay the same in every theme, so they always mean the same thing.

sections.title: Look
sections.text:
- Orbit: Soft corners, hairline borders. The default.
- Crisp: Square corners, firm outlines, ruled lists.
- Soft: Round pills, no outlines, cards lifted by shadow.
- Terminal: Mono everywhere, sharp corners, dashed rules.
- Editorial: Serif headings, open layout, underlined tabs.
- Compact: Icon sidebar, tight rows, the most on screen.
- TUI: Boxed panels, inverse selection and [x] checks.
Picking Compact also switches the sidebar to icons; you can switch it back with the Sidebar setting. Density stays its own setting and works with every look.
A look reaches every page: in Terminal and TUI every corner is square, Crisp keeps them nearly square, and the shapes inside controls follow (a switch's knob and a slider's handle turn square with them). Lists, tabs, steps, checkboxes and radios show what's selected the look's way (in TUI a checkbox reads [x] and a radio (*)).

sections.title: Accent colour
sections.text:
Accent color starts on Theme's own, which follows the colour theme. The presets are Indigo, Violet, Teal, Rose and Amber, and Custom opens a picker for any colour. A preset or custom accent you pick is kept when you change the colour theme. High contrast keeps its own accent so its text stays readable; your pick comes back when you leave it.
Themes change the manager, and the Community tab follows them: it takes the colour theme, the look and light or dark, and changes with them. The canvas nodes keep ComfyUI's colours, so they sit well next to other nodes.

pages.title: Glossary
pages.blurb: The words you'll see in these docs, one line each.

sections.title: Terms
sections.text:
Module
One piece you build in the manager, such as a wildcard or a fixed value. It lives in your library and you can add it to any WP Context.
Library
Everything you've saved in the manager: modules, bundles and templates.
$variable
A named value, such as $subject. Modules write variables; your template reads them.
Wildcard
A list of options. Each run picks one and writes it to a $variable.
Weight
How likely an option is next to the others. Weight 2 comes up twice as often as weight 1; 0 switches it off.
Null option
A wildcard option that prints nothing, for "sometimes leave this out".
Fallback
The option a wildcard uses when nothing else is left to pick, for example after a constraint ruled everything out.
Sub-category (tag)
A label on a wildcard option, such as "warm". Filters and constraints work with tags.
Tag group
Tags sorted under a name, such as species or temperature. A group is either classify (the tags describe the option) or accepts (see below).
Accepts group
A tag group whose tags are choices the option offers, such as shoes that go with an outfit. One is rolled with each pick, and $outfit.SHOES prints it.
Library tag
A label on a whole module, bundle or template, used only to organise your library. It never changes a pick.
Fixed Values
A module that sets variables to text you type. Nothing is rolled.
Combine
A module that builds a new variable from text and other variables, such as "$style portrait of $subject".
Derivation
A module with if/then rules: when a variable says one thing, set another variable.
Constraint
A module that changes a later wildcard's odds based on an earlier pick, such as "ocean makes stormy likelier".
Bundle
Several modules saved together, so you can add them to a WP Context in one go.
Template
Your prompt with $variables in it, such as "a $style portrait of $subject". The WP Prompt Assembler fills it in.
Reference (@{…})
A fresh pick from another wildcard, written inside an option. Type @ to insert one.
Chip
The small pill a text field shows for a $variable or an @{…} reference. A red one points at something missing.
Inline choice ({a|b})
A quick random choice written straight into an option, fixed value or combine. Picks one of the parts each run. The Assembler prints it as typed.
Seed
The number behind every random pick. Same seed and same modules give the same result.
WP Context
The node that holds your modules, rolls them on every Generate and passes the variables on.
Chaining
Wiring one WP Context into another. The second starts with the first one's variables and can add to or replace them.
Hide from prompt
A variable that prints nothing, while other modules can still use it. The globe button on a row.
Lock pick
Keeps the same pick on every Generate until you unlock it.
Hold across run
The same pick on every frame of one loop run, and a new one next Generate.
Negative
Words that go to the negative prompt when a variable is printed. Options, fixed values, combines and derivations can carry them.
Loop
The WP Context Loop node: runs your pipeline several times in one Generate, one frame each.

pages.title: Make variations in one click
pages.blurb: Several prompts and images from one Generate, or every combination of a few options.

sections.title: Several random variations
sections.text:
- Add a WP Context Loop and wire its context output into your first WP Context's upstream input.
- Set count to how many variations you want, say 4.
- Add a WP Seed List: wire the loop's loop_config into it and its seed output into your sampler's seed.
- Press Generate once. You get four prompts and four images.
Figure: WP Context Loop (count 4) → WP Context → WP Prompt Assembler using $iteration of $iteration_total → one prompt per frame. Screenshot of a four-node loop chain. A WP Context Loop (seed 42, fixed, count 4, strategy hash, Edit frame chips base and #1 to #4, iteration var $iteration) feeds a WP Context holding Starter subject and Starter style, which feeds a WP Prompt Assembler with the template '$iteration of $iteration_total: a picture of a $subject, in the style of $style' and chips $iteration, $iteration_total, $subject and $style. A Preview as Text node shows the run's prompts, starting '1 of 4: a picture of a wolf, in the style of oil painting' and '2 of 4: a picture of a dog, in the style of oil painting'. One prompt per frame.
Skip the Seed List and the sampler uses the same seed for every frame, so two frames with the same prompt give the same image.

sections.title: Every combination of a few options
sections.text: To compare options side by side, open Sweep combinations on the loop, switch it on and add the wildcards to sweep. Three hair colours against two moods make six frames, one per pair. Keep the sampler on one fixed seed so only the prompt changes. More on WP Context Loop.

sections.title: Keep one thing the same across the batch
sections.text: Switch on Hold across run on a row, such as the character, and every frame keeps that pick while the rest changes. The next Generate picks a new one. See Keep something the same.

sections.title: Number the frames
sections.text: $iteration is the frame number and $iteration_total the count. They're hidden from the prompt until you click their globe and Σ buttons on the loop. A derivation can also test $iteration to tell a story over the frames.

pages.title: Make two picks agree
pages.blurb: Stop clashes: let one pick steer another with a constraint, an accepts group or a derivation.

sections.title: Pick the right tool
sections.text:
Constraint
One pick changes the odds of another: winter rules out summer clothes, stormy makes moody likelier. The usual answer.
Accepts tag group
The matching choice travels with the option: each outfit lists the shoes that go with it, and $outfit.SHOES prints one of them.
Derivation
Adds or changes text after a pick: if $season is winter, add "a scarf". Use it for text, not for steering another pick.
Reference with a filter
An option draws from another wildcard, narrowed by tags: "@{Color:warm} jeans". Good when the match is always the same.

sections.title: With a constraint
sections.text:
- Tag the options of both wildcards, for example the season wildcard with winter and summer, the outfit wildcard with warm and light.
- Create a Constraint. Source: the season wildcard. Target: the outfit wildcard.
- In the rule matrix set winter × light to Exclude, and summer × warm too. Use Boost or Reduce for a nudge instead of a ban.
- On the WP Context, put the constraint between the two wildcards: season, then constraint, then outfit.
Figure: Source wildcard, then the constraint, then the target wildcard. The #1 badges link the constraint to its target. Screenshot of a WP Context (modules 3 / 3) wired into a WP Prompt Assembler. The Context rows, top to bottom: Starter subject ('$subject · 4 options'), Starter pairing, a constraint marked #1-all ('$subject → $mood · 2×2'), and Starter mood marked #1 ('$mood · 4 options'). The Assembler's template is 'a $mood $subject, masterpiece' and its preview reads 'a sleepy wolf, masterpiece'. It shows the order: source wildcard, then the constraint, then the target wildcard it changes.
Give the target a fallback option, so a combination you didn't plan for still prints something. The constraint's Preview shows the odds for every pair before you run.
For a strict pairing, such as "maid always wears the frilled apron", use an Only rule. More on Constraint.

sections.title: When the deciding value isn't a pick
sections.text: Constraints react to picks. To steer from a variable, such as the loaded model from WP Model Info, make a wildcard whose options spell the variable's values and set Match variable on it. It then picks the matching option and can be a constraint's source.

sections.title: Check it
sections.text: Run the Test Runner over a few hundred seeds: the Samples tab shows every pair that came up. Or wire a WP Debug and look at the Trace tab to see which constraint changed which odds. A constraint that did nothing shows Constraint never applied; that usually means it sits in the wrong place. $season and $outfit here are only examples.

pages.title: Keep something the same
pages.blurb: Keep a style, a character or a whole prompt while the rest changes.

sections.title: Choose how long it should stay
sections.text:
Keep one pick for good: Lock pick
Click the lock on a row (Lock seed on modules other than wildcards). It keeps its result on every Generate until you unlock it. Good for a style you've settled on.
Keep one pick for a batch: Hold across run
Right-click a row, or switch it on in the row's editor. Every loop frame of one Generate shares the pick; the next Generate picks again. Good for one character through a story.
Always the same option: untick the others
In the row's editor, untick every option but one. Or use a Fixed Values module if it never changes at all.
Keep every pick: fix the Context seed
Set the WP Context's seed to fixed (control after generate). The same seed and the same modules give the same prompt every time.
Keep the image too: fix the sampler seed
The prompt and the sampler have separate seeds. For the same image, fix both. With a loop, lock the seeds in WP Seed List.
Keep one frame: lock it on that frame
With a loop, pick the frame's chip and lock the row there. Only that frame keeps its pick.
Found a prompt you like? In WP Debug, note the Context's seed and put it back in the seed box later, or lock the rows that matter. The Test Runner's Copy seed does the same for a seed you found there.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
- A lock keeps the module's dice the same. If you edit its options, or a constraint above it changes the odds, the result can still change. Hold across run keeps the finished text instead.
- Hide from prompt and Hold across run apply to every frame, so they're greyed out while you edit a single frame.
- The full story of seeds is on Seeds & loops.

pages.title: Share a pack or workflow
pages.blurb: Send a workflow, export modules to a file, or publish to the community.

sections.title: Share a workflow
sections.text:
Save the workflow in ComfyUI as usual and send the file. Every row on a WP Context is a copy of the module, so the workflow runs on another machine even if that library is empty.
- An @{…} reference looks on the node first, then in the library. Keep every wildcard a reference needs on the node (switched off is fine) and it works anywhere.
- The person you send it to sees missing on rows they don't have. Right-click → Save to library adds them.
- Per-frame changes and the loop's settings are saved in the workflow too.

sections.title: Share modules as a file
sections.text:
- In the manager open Import / Export → Export.
- Tick what to share: the whole library, a kind, or single modules and bundles. Select with dependencies adds the wildcards they reference.
- Download the file and send it.
To bring one in, use the Import tab: pick the file or paste its text, choose what to add, and decide what happens when a name already exists. An import can be undone from the message that follows.

sections.title: Publish to the community
sections.text:
On a module or bundle, the Publish to community button opens the publish form with everything filled in; the Export tab has the same button for a selection. Others find it in the Community tab and install it in one click, with the wildcards it needs.
A pack that uses a newer feature asks people on an older version to update before it installs, so nothing gets dropped on the way.

sections.title: Coming from A1111 or Forge
sections.text: Text and YAML wildcard packs import directly: see Import wildcard packs.

sections.title: Related
sections.text: Bundles Import wildcard packs Recommended pack structure

pages.title: Fix common problems
pages.blurb: Something prints nothing, never changes, or won't install: causes and fixes.

sections.title: Something prints wrong
sections.text:
A $variable prints nothing (MISSING VAR)
Nothing before the Assembler sets it, the name is misspelt, or it's hidden (the globe on its row is on). WP Model Info and the loop's $iteration are hidden by default.
A wildcard prints nothing
It picked its null option, a constraint ruled out every option, or a tag filter matched none. Give it a fallback option; WP Debug's Warnings tab says which it was.
{a|b} prints as typed
The Assembler doesn't roll anything. Put the choice in a wildcard, fixed value or combine and print its variable.
@{…} prints nothing
References only work in wildcard options and derivation actions. In a combine or the Assembler they print nothing.
$name in a wildcard option prints as typed
Options and fixed values can't read variables. Use a Combine below them.
Commas or words go missing around an empty variable
The Assembler tidies the commas and joining words around a variable that came out empty. Write the template so it still reads well when something is empty.

sections.title: Picks don't change the way you expect
sections.text:
The same prompt every Generate
The Context's seed is set to fixed, or the rows are locked or hold their pick. Set the seed to randomize, or unlock the rows.
Every loop frame gives the same image
The sampler uses one seed for all frames. Add a WP Seed List between the loop and the sampler.
A constraint does nothing
Check the order: source wildcard, then the constraint, then the target. WP Debug's Trace tab shows whether it applied; Constraint never applied means the target didn't run after it.
An option never comes up
Its weight is 0, it's unticked on the node, a constraint excludes it, or a filter leaves it out. The Test Runner shows each option's share over many seeds.
A later Context undoes my pick
When two Contexts set the same variable, the later one wins. The row shows a blue dot for this.

sections.title: Library and packs
sections.text:
A row says missing
The module isn't in your library, often because the workflow came from someone else. It still works; right-click → Save to library to keep it.
A row says drift (library updated on a bundle)
You changed the library entry after adding it. Right-click → Refresh from library (Reset to library snapshot on a bundle) to take the change.
A pack won't install and asks for an update
It uses a feature from a newer version. Update Wildcard Pipeline and try again.
A constraint shows a missing wildcard
Open it and use Reattach to point it at a wildcard you have, or Download from community.
Undo a change to the library
Settings › Library & data › Backups lists every backup; Restore puts one back the next time ComfyUI starts, after backing up the current library. Backups to keep keeps the newest ones, the ones you make yourself too. Pin a backup (the bookmark button) to keep it for good: pinned ones are never deleted for you and don't count toward the limit. A row marked Removed at next backup goes the next time a backup is made. Type a short note next to Back up now to tell your own backups apart.

sections.title: Still stuck?
sections.text: Every warning is explained on Warning & conflict types. Problems with the AI assistant have their own page: Troubleshooting.

pages.title: AI assistant
pages.blurb: Optional and off by default: what the assistant does and where to start.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
The assistant uses a model you bring: one running on your own PC (Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp or any OpenAI-compatible server) or the Claude or OpenAI API with your own key. Wildcard Pipeline ships no model and sends nothing anywhere until you turn the assistant on.
Once it's on, you can:
- Draft in the editors. Press AI in any editor to write new wildcard options, rules, fixed values, combines or templates, or to rewrite, retag and re-weight what's there.
- Chat. Ask about your library or how something works, or ask for a change. Every change comes back as a card you apply or dismiss.
- Build a whole pack from one description: the wildcards, rules, template and a bundle, tested on the engine before you install them.
- Organize your library: descriptions, tags, categories and ratings.
- Ask about a Test Runner run: why an option never comes up, or how to fix a warning.
- Look things up on the web or on Danbooru, if you set that up. It asks before each search.
Every request includes the item's name, description and tags, so a good description points the model the right way.

sections.title: Start here
sections.text:
- Set up a model: pick a provider and a model, then press Test connection.
- Open a wildcard and press AI above its options. Draft with AI shows the rest of the editor tools.
- Press AI in the top bar to open the chat.
- When you're ready for more, try the Pack builder.

sections.title: You stay in control
sections.text:
- Nothing is saved until you press Apply, Add or Save. Most changes have Undo.
- It can't delete anything unless you allow it in Settings, and every delete asks you first.
- It only goes online through web search, and asks before each search.
Details are on Privacy and safety.

sections.title: Which model?
sections.text: Any model can draft options. Rules, chat and the pack builder need a model that follows instructions well. A 9B model on a 16 GB card can run the chat. Claude and OpenAI don't write explicit content, so for NSFW packs run an uncensored model yourself. Set up a model lists suggestions, and Troubleshooting helps when a small model struggles.

pages.title: Set up a model
pages.blurb: Turn the assistant on, connect a server or API key, and pick a model.

sections.title: Connect in four steps
sections.text:
- Open Settings → AI assistant and switch on Enable.
- Pick a Provider: Ollama, LM Studio, llama.cpp, Claude, OpenAI, or Other for any OpenAI-compatible server. The server address is filled in for you.
- For Claude or OpenAI, paste your API key. A local server doesn't need one.
- Pick a Model from the list your server reports, then press Test connection.
Test connection lists the models, asks the chosen one for a tiny answer and tells you whether it worked and how long it took. It also checks that the model has enough room (context) for the chat, and warns when it doesn't.
Figure: Settings › AI assistant: the switch that turns it on, the provider buttons, and the server address, model and API key fields. Screenshot of the manager's Settings › AI assistant page. Turn on the AI assistant is off ('Off by default, and nothing is sent anywhere until you turn it on'). Under Provider are buttons Claude, OpenAI and OpenRouter (CLOUD) and Ollama (selected), LM Studio, llama.cpp and Other (OpenAI-compatible) (LOCAL). Below are Server address (http://127.0.0.1:11434), Model (with a refresh button), API key ('Not needed for Ollama') and Test connection.
Load local models with at least 16k of context; that is the minimum. 32k or more is recommended for chats that take several steps, which often reach 20k to 26k on a 27B model. In LM Studio that's the Context Length in the model's load settings; load the model again after you change it.

sections.title: The basic settings
sections.text:
Enable
Turns the assistant on. While it is off, the AI buttons are hidden and nothing is sent anywhere.
Provider
Each provider remembers its own address, model and key, so you can switch back and forth. A key icon means a key is saved. The settings that depend on the model are kept for each model too (see below).
Server address
Change it if your server runs on another port or machine.
API key
Stored on the ComfyUI side and never shown again; Remove deletes it. A key is only sent to the address it was saved for.
Model
Picked from your server's list (refresh after downloading a new one), or typed in.
Unload after
For local servers: how long an idle model stays loaded, so ComfyUI gets the GPU memory back. From right after each answer up to 1 hour, or Custom.
About my library
A short note (up to 600 characters) every chat, Draft with AI and Pack builder request reads. Suggest drafts one from your library. See the Chat page.
Thinking
How much a thinking model reasons before it answers. The list shows what the chosen model takes: Off and On for a model with an on/off switch, or its own levels (Low to Max) for a model with levels, and a line under it says which. The same picker sits in the chat header. For a small or medium local model, As the model does means Off, and a choice you pick holds for the whole answer (switching between steps made LM Studio re-read the whole prompt).
Each setting shows its Recommended value under it, and lists mark the recommended choice. Reset to recommended puts every AI setting back after showing what will change; your provider, keys, addresses and chosen models stay as they are. Context is the one exception: Reset raises a window under 16k to 32k and leaves a bigger one alone.
Kept for each model. Thinking, Model size, Most context to use, Tool format, Sampling, Choose the tool first and Short tool list are saved for the provider and model you set them on, and Unload after for the provider. Switch from Claude at Medium thinking to a Qwen in LM Studio and you get the Qwen's own settings back, not Claude's. A model you haven't used yet keeps the provider's values but starts Thinking and Model size at automatic, since another model's level or size may not fit it. Permissions, web search, the About my library note and the chat display options are the same for every provider.
Advanced settings
Model size
How much the assistant asks of the model. Small models (under 20B) get shorter instructions, smaller tool results and the extra help described on Troubleshooting. Automatic reads the size from the model's name; set it when the name doesn't say.
Most context to use
Tokens of context the assistant uses (16384 by default; presets 4k to 128k, or Custom). 16k is the minimum and 32k is recommended for chats that take several steps. Ollama gets exactly this much, because its own default is far smaller and silently cuts the instructions off. Lower it if the model no longer fits on your GPU. A new chat also checks how much context the model really has and starts leaner when it is tight.
Tool format
How the chat calls its tools. Native tool calls are what most models are trained for; JSON steps work with any model. Automatic uses JSON steps for small and medium local models (a 9B on LM Studio did twice as well that way) and for any server that refuses or garbles native calls. A chat keeps the format it started with.
Choose the tool first
Off by default. A small or medium model names the tool it will call, then writes only that tool's arguments. Some models pick better this way; each step is a little slower.
Short tool list
Off by default. A small model in JSON steps gets one line per tool in its instructions, and a tool's full description (its arguments and an example) the first time a step offers it. About 2,000 fewer tokens per step, which helps when the context is tight. Applies to new chats.
Debug log
Off by default. Records every AI request you make in this browser: each model call with the prompt as sent, the reply, thinking, tool calls and tokens. A Debug button in the top bar lists them with Copy debug, a readable copy to paste into a bug report. Images are left out (only their size is noted) and keys are hidden. Copies are also saved in the ai-debug folder of the Wildcard Pipeline data folder; the last 300 are kept.
Sampling
Optional top K, top P, min P, repeat penalty and presence penalty, sent with every request to a local or OpenAI-compatible server. Empty uses the server's own setting for the model (LM Studio's, Ollama's). The assistant still sets the temperature itself, low for tool steps. Claude and OpenAI's own API get none. For Qwen 3.5 and later, top K 20, top P 0.8, min P 0 and repeat penalty 1.0 follow the model card.
Embedding model
Under Search. Turns on meaning search, so “warm colors” finds a wildcard of amber and crimson. Pick a small embedding model such as nomic-embed-text or embeddinggemma (Ollama) or text-embedding-3-small (OpenAI). Off by default; word search already covers most questions. Claude has no embeddings.
Embedding server
Leave empty to use the server above. A llama.cpp server only serves embeddings when started with --embeddings, so run a second one and put its address here.
Library index
How many items the chat's search index holds. It lives next to your library database (wildcard-pipeline.ai-index.db) and keeps itself up to date; Rebuild builds it again. When the embedding server stops answering (LM Studio closed, say), it says meaning search is paused and why, prints that once in the ComfyUI console, and tries again on its own after 30 seconds, then waiting longer each time up to 10 minutes. Word search keeps working meanwhile; Rebuild or a working Test connection tries at once.
Keys from the environment work too: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY and OPENAI_API_KEY only go to Claude's or OpenAI's own address; WP_AI_API_KEY goes to the provider's usual address, or to the one in WP_AI_API_KEY_HOST. Change the server address and a saved key stays saved but isn't sent until you paste it again or change the address back.
Test connection also shows how many tokens every new chat starts with (instructions, tool list and your library summary), and for small models it tries one tool step. If the server still says a request is too long, the chat tries once more with less and otherwise tells you how much context to load the model with.
OpenAI is reached through its Responses API, which its newest models need for tool calls; their reasoning is carried between steps in encrypted form.
Thinking per model. The assistant asks the server what the model takes: LM Studio and Ollama list each model's options, OpenRouter and Claude list each model's levels, and OpenAI models are known by name. A model with only on and off (Qwen 3 under LM Studio, most Ollama models) shows Off and On; a level you picked for another model counts as On. A model that must think (the newest Claude and GPT models) has no Off, so Off asks for its lowest level. A level a model doesn't have becomes the nearest one it has. If the server refuses a choice, the assistant asks again without it and remembers that for the model. If thinking uses up a whole reply, it asks again with thinking off and keeps it off for that model until you change Thinking.
Draft with AI panels. The panels in the editors (Add, Remove, Rewrite, Retag and Weights on a wildcard, and the rule, text, description and organize panels) write short, checked answers, so with Thinking on Auto a local model answers them without thinking. Pick On or a level to have it think there too. A model that keeps thinking for about 4,000 tokens without starting its answer is stopped and asked again without thinking, and the working line counts its thinking as it goes.
LM Studio turns a model's thinking only on or off: it never hands a level to the model's chat template. A template with its own levels (Qwen 3.8: low, medium, xhigh) then always runs at its default, so On there means the template's default effort. llama.cpp does hand the level to the template.
To get the levels in LM Studio, give the model a small model.yaml that declares them. Make a folder such as ~/.lmstudio/hub/models/you/qwen3.8-27b-effort/ with a model.yaml whose base names the GGUF you already have, and add two customFields entries, each with the effect setJinjaVariable: a boolean on enable_thinking (without it, thinking can't be turned off) and a select on reasoning_effort with the template's levels (low, medium, xhigh). It shows up as a second model that uses the same file, so nothing is stored twice. LM Studio then lists its levels and the Thinking picker offers them. A level only counts while thinking is on: in LM Studio's own chat, turn its Thinking switch on as well. The new model doesn't take the old one's load settings, so put its context length, KV cache and thinking budget in the yaml too (a config section), or a full-precision cache can make it too slow to answer.

sections.title: Which model
sections.text:
Settings › AI assistant › Suggested models lists picks for the provider you chose. Only the ones marked Tested were tried with Wildcard Pipeline; the rest come from benchmarks and community reports.
- Claude or OpenAI are good for organizing, rules and safe packs (GPT-6 Luna is plenty; GPT-6.1 Sol costs more and isn't needed). They don't allow explicit writing.
- OpenRouter reaches many more models, most paid with credits, including unmoderated ones.
- Your own server: the list names the model only, in two groups. Which build you download is up to you: who uploaded it, the quant, and whether it is uncensored ("heretic" and "abliterated" builds have refusals removed). None is proven to know Danbooru tags, so check a draft before relying on it.
For the chat and packs. Tested with Wildcard Pipeline. Any of these can be your only model.
- Qwen3.6 35B A3B (16 GB GPU): The one we use most, for chat, packs and writing. Mixture of experts, so it stays fast with part of it in system RAM: about 50 tok/s on a 16 GB card with 32 GB RAM.
- Qwen3.8 27B (16-24 GB GPU): The best at following instructions. A 3-bit file fits a 16 GB card, 24 GB is comfortable. Slower than the 35B A3B.
- Qwen3.5 9B (8 GB GPU): Fits 8 to 12 GB, or beside ComfyUI. Fine for single items, tags and negatives; it misses parts of bigger asks with several items.
For writing options. Not tested here. They can't call tools, so keep them for drafting.
- Cydonia 24B (16 GB GPU): Suggested because community reports rate it highly for explicit creative writing that still follows instructions (a Mistral Small 24B fine-tune).
- Gemma 4 31B (24 GB GPU): Suggested because the UGI benchmark puts its uncensored builds first for world knowledge among writers.
Search the name in Ollama, LM Studio or Hugging Face and pick a build that fits your GPU.
With two models, keep a writer selected for drafting and switch to a chat model when you organize, chat or build a whole pack.
In Ollama, a Qwen 3.5 / 3.6 model pulled straight from Hugging Face (ollama pull hf.co/…) misses Ollama's tool-call reader, so tool calls can come back as plain text. Fix: make a file named Modelfile holding
Modelfile:
FROM hf.co/<repo>:<quant>
RENDERER qwen3.5
PARSER qwen3.5
run ollama create my-model -f Modelfile and pick my-model. For Gemma 4 use RENDERER gemma4-large (or gemma4-small below 12B) and PARSER gemma4. Ollama's own qwen3.5 and gemma4 models already have it.
