pages.blurb: Give one loop frame its own settings: a fixed pick, a locked seed, a module switched off.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A WP Context Loop runs your Contexts several times, one frame each. Normally every frame uses the same settings, called the base. An override changes something for one frame only. Think of it as a keyframe: most frames follow the base, and you change just the ones that need it.
Figure: Each frame starts from the base, then that frame's overrides are applied on top. Steps: Base settings (apply to all frames) → default → Frame #k override (changes just frame k) → per-frame change → Each frame (base, except where overridden). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: Base settings (apply to all frames), an arrow labelled default, Frame #k override (patches just frame k), an arrow labelled per-frame patch, and Resolved frames (base, except where overridden). Caption: each frame resolves from the base, then any override recorded for that frame is layered on top, like a keyframe that changes only the frames you override.

sections.title: Editing a frame
sections.text:
The loop has an Edit frame row of chips: base, then #1 #2 #3 …. Click a frame chip and every row editor now edits that frame: what you change is saved for that frame only. Click base to go back to editing all frames.
Figure: The loop's Edit frame chips (base, #1 to #4) above the Context it drives. Screenshot of a WP Context Loop (seed 42, fixed, count 4) wired into a WP Context (Starter subject and Hair) and a WP Prompt Assembler ('a $subject with $hair', preview 'a wolf with black hair'). On the loop, the Edit frame row shows the chips base (selected), #1, #2, #3 and #4, with the hint 'Alt-click locks a seed · Ctrl-click bypasses'. Below are Override Context seed (off), the iteration var $iteration with its globe and Σ buttons, and Bypass loop (off).
A frame keeps only what you changed. Rows with a change show a badge, and Revert to base clears a frame's changes. Adding or removing options, or anything else that changes the module itself, always edits the base.

sections.title: What you can change per frame
sections.text:
Wildcard options
Which options a frame may pick, their weights, or the tag filter. Tick only "red" on frame #3 and that frame is red while the others stay random. A constraint can still rule a ticked option out, so keep a fallback.
Combine template or fixed value
A frame's own text, such as a different caption on the last frame.
Constraint
Its reach and rules for one frame.
Lock pick
Lock a pick on one frame only. See below.
On / off
Run a module on some frames only. See below.
Frame changes live in the workflow. They aren't saved in bundles, and the Test Runner doesn't use them. For a frame rule you can share, use a wildcard with Match variable on iteration plus a constraint, or a derivation that tests $iteration. See Recommended pack structure.
Good for
- A few named beats on one canvas (frame #1 is the establishing shot)
Better with something else
- A pattern over all frames: a derivation on $iteration
- Anything you'll share: frame changes aren't saved in bundles

sections.title: Switch a module on or off per frame
sections.text:
The tick box on a row works per frame too. A frame uses its own setting if it has one, otherwise the base. So both of these work:
- On in the base, off on a frame: the module runs everywhere except that frame.
- Off in the base, on on a frame: the module only runs on that frame, so an extra element shows up just there.
A frame with a module off still makes an image; the module just adds nothing. WP Debug shows whether a module was off for that frame or off everywhere.

sections.title: Lock a pick on one frame
sections.text:
Lock a row while a frame chip is active and only that frame keeps its pick; the others still change. Lock it on base to keep it on every frame. Unlocking on one frame while the base is locked frees just that frame.
Hide from prompt and Hold across run apply to every frame, so they're greyed out while a frame chip is active. Switch back to base to change them.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Context Loop Seeds & loops WP Context

pages.title: Constraints in depth
pages.blurb: How constraints combine, which uses they reach, and how they work across Contexts.

sections.title: Before you read this
sections.text: This page builds on the Constraint page, which covers making a constraint, the rule modes, Only, the preview and the order in the stack. You only need what's below when one wildcard is used several times, constraints overlap, or you use tag axes.

sections.title: Several constraints on one target
sections.text: Every constraint that reaches a target applies, and their effects multiply: a ×3 boost and a ×0.5 reduce give ×1.5. An Exclude from any of them wins. You can add several constraints for the same source and target, one per rule, each with its own reach.

sections.title: How far a constraint reaches
sections.text:
A constraint isn't used up after one pick. By default it changes the odds of every use of its target below it in the run, including uses inside references. Each use of a constraint in a Context has a Target reach setting to narrow that:
All
The default. Every use of the target below the constraint.
First
Only the first use below it; later ones roll freely.
Next N
The next N uses below it (you set N); the rest roll freely.
Pick
Only the uses you tick from a list of the ones it can reach.
Reach only looks downwards: First and Next N count from the constraint's own position. Pick names each use by its row, or, for a use inside a reference, by the row and option that hold the reference.
If a constraint reaches nothing (its only target sits above it, the count is larger than what's below, or a picked row is gone), the canvas flags it so a dead pairing doesn't go unnoticed. If it reaches fewer uses than Next N or Pick asked for, WP Debug notes a partial reach after the run.

sections.title: Targets used inside references
sections.text: If the target wildcard only appears inside another wildcard's option text, as an @{…} reference, the constraint still applies: it follows the reference to find the target. Each such use counts once for the reach setting, even when several references lead to it.

sections.title: Tag axes on either side
sections.text:
A tag group marked accepts (an axis, read as $var.AXIS) lists alternatives: one of its tags is rolled per pick. Constraints treat it so the tag you read always agrees with the tag the constraint acts on.
- Accepts source. The constraint uses the one tag that was rolled, not every tag on the option. An outfit tagged sneakers · heels · sandals that rolls sandals makes a “same tag wins” matrix pin the target to sandals, so $outfit.SHOES and the shoe that gets picked match.
- Classify source (the default kind): all the option's tags apply together. With a strict diagonal matrix, an option carrying several tags can rule out the whole target.
- Accepts target. A target option stays in the pool if the source allows any of its axis tags, and its own axis roll is then limited to the allowed tag. A shoe tagged sandals · heels isn't dropped because heels is excluded; it stays and rolls sandals.
An accepts source, an accepts target and a diagonal matrix together make $source.AXIS equal $target.AXIS on every run.

sections.title: Constraints across chained Contexts
sections.text: A constraint in one Context also applies to its target in a later, chained Context. You can keep all your pairing rules in a separate "constraints" Context placed before the one with the wildcards.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: Constraint Wildcard Context chaining

pages.title: Hidden variables
pages.blurb: Hide a $variable from the prompt while other modules still use it.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
Click the globe on a row (or switch on Hide from prompt in its editor) and the row's variables print nothing in the prompt. Combines, derivations, constraints and later Contexts can still read them. The docs and older messages also call this internal.
An example: a hidden $season wildcard picks "winter". A combine below it writes $coat as "a $season coat", and a derivation sets $weather to "snowing" when the season is winter. The prompt gets the coat and the weather, but never the bare word "winter".
Good for
- A pick that decides other picks but shouldn't print, like a season, a class or a rating level
- Numbers a WP Var node reads
Better with something else
- Leaving a variable out of one template: just don't write it in that template

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
- A hidden variable stays hidden through chained Contexts. Only the Assembler drops it, so a later Context can still read it.
- Hiding belongs to the row that wrote the value. If a later module writes the same variable without hiding it, it prints again.
- Written in an Assembler template, a hidden variable prints nothing and shows as missing. To print something built from it, use a combine and print the combine's variable.
- A hidden variable adds nothing to the Assembler's negative output.
- WP Context Loop's $iteration and $iteration_total are hidden by default. Click their globe buttons on the loop to print them, for example to caption a frame "1 of 4".
- WP Model Info's variables are hidden by default too; switch them on the same way.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: Context chaining WP Prompt Assembler Combine

pages.title: Negatives
pages.blurb: Send words to the negative prompt from the option, value or rule that needs them.

sections.title: The idea
sections.text:
A negative belongs to the $variable it came with, and only reaches an Assembler that prints that variable. The main Assembler that prints $hair, $mood and $face gets all three negatives; a face detailer Assembler that prints only $face gets only the face words.
Figure: Negative words only reach an Assembler that printed their variable. Steps: Wildcard option (negative: fruit) → picked → $hair (carries it) → used → Assembler (prints $hair) → collected → negative output (fruit). Flow diagram of four stages left to right: a Wildcard option carrying 'negative: fruit', an arrow labelled picked, the variable $hair (carries it), an arrow labelled used, the Assembler (renders $hair), an arrow labelled collected, and the negative output (fruit). Caption: negatives follow usage, so words only reach an Assembler's negative output when their variable was rendered by its template.

sections.title: Where negatives come from
sections.text:
Wildcard option
Each option has a Negative line under its value. When the option is picked, its words go with the wildcard's variable. With several picks, each pick brings its own. The null option has none.
Fixed value
Same Negative line. A fixed value always applies, so its negative always comes along: a $style of "oil painting" can bring "photo, 3d render". On a Context node each row shows its negative under the value; change it there for that node only, and the reset button brings back the library's.
Combine
A combine brings along the negatives of every variable it reads, with no setup. It can also have a Negative of its own for the phrase as a whole, which you can change per node too.
Derivation
Two extra actions: Add to negative keeps the variable's text and adds words to its negative ("when $mood is gloomy, add smiling"). Replace negative swaps its negative for new words. Use + And to change the text and the negative in one rule.
WP Context Injector row
A row can have a Negative, which can use the row's input. It replaces any negative the variable had before.

sections.title: What you can write in a negative
sections.text:
A negative takes the same syntax as the value next to it.
Field | Accepts
Wildcard option negative | text, {a|b}, @{ref} (no $vars)
Fixed value negative | text, {a|b} (no refs, no $vars)
Combine negative | $vars, {a|b}
Derivation “Add to negative” value | $vars, @{ref}, {a|b}
Injector row negative | the row's input, like the row template
Assembler negative template | $vars and $negatives (where the collected words go)
Negatives never change your picks. Adding or editing one leaves every seed's prompt exactly as it was. A reference inside a negative rolls on its own and isn't counted as a pick: it doesn't show in the Test Runner, doesn't trigger constraints, and brings no negative of its own.

sections.title: How they follow the variable
sections.text:
Setting a variable drops its old negative
When a module writes a variable again, the old negative goes with the old value. Append and Prepend keep it and add the new one.
One pick, one negative
$props.0 brings only the first pick's negative. $props and $props.GROUP bring every pick's.
Hidden variables add nothing
A hidden variable never prints, so its negative never reaches the negative output. Later modules that read it still get it.
Words you type in the negative template
A $variable you write in the Assembler's negative template adds its text, not its negative.
Reading a negative: $name.neg
$pose.neg is the negative $pose has at that point, and $props.1.neg the second pick's. Use it like any variable: in a combine, in the Assembler's negative template, in a derivation's "if", or to copy one variable's negative to another with Add to negative. Reading .neg doesn't count as printing $pose, so its words don't come in twice.

sections.title: The Assembler's negative output
sections.text:
WP Prompt Assembler has a second output, negative. Wire it into your negative CLIP Text Encode. Its negative template sits in a fold-out section under the preview:
Figure: The Assembler's negative preview and output next to the prompt. Screenshot of a WP Context (seed 3) holding Hair, Weather and Quality, wired into a WP Prompt Assembler whose prompt and negative outputs each feed a Preview as Text node. The template is '$quality, a woman with $hair, $weather'; the preview reads 'masterpiece, best quality, a woman with black hair, clear sky'. The negative template is empty ('just the variables' negatives'), and the negative preview, marked '1 from variables', reads 'lowres, bad anatomy', which came from the Quality fixed value. The negative Preview as Text prints 'lowres, bad anatomy'.
- $negatives marks where the collected words go, e.g. lowres, bad anatomy, $negatives.
- An empty template outputs just the collected words.
- Without $negatives, the collected words go at the end.
Repeated words are dropped, also when written differently: (blurry:1.2) counts as blurry, and so does one you already typed in the template.

sections.title: Cleaning both prompts
sections.text: WP Prompt Cleaner has an optional negative input and a cleaned negative output. Its rule list has a second column for the negative, which follows the prompt's preset except fuzzy dedupe and the blocklist. Switch on Drop negative tags also in prompt to remove a word from the negative when the prompt asks for it; the report names the overlap either way.

sections.title: Bulk add
sections.text:
In a wildcard's bulk add, -- starts an option's negative. Everything after the first -- is the negative, and #tag / *N still work at the end of either side:
Module | Line
Wildcard | strawberry blonde #warm *2 -- strawberry, fruit
Fixed values | style = oil painting -- photo, 3d render
With options checked, bulk edit's Negative menu adds words to each checked option, replaces their negative, or clears it.

sections.title: Seeing where each word came from
sections.text: WP Debug lists each variable's negative under its value, and names the module when the words came from somewhere else (a derivation, or a combine reading $hair). The Test Runner shows a NEG line under each output, coloured by the variable each word came from, and a Negative column in Samples.

sections.title: Sharing
sections.text: A pack that uses negatives needs an extension version that knows them. An older version asks you to update instead of dropping the words.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Prompt Assembler WP Prompt Cleaner Wildcard Derivation

pages.title: Conflicts & warnings
pages.blurb: Where warnings show, what the colours mean. Nothing here stops a run.

sections.title: Where you'll see them
sections.text:
- On the node, while you build. A WP Context shows a small coloured dot and a short label on the row, such as MISSING VAR. Hover it for the message. A subgraph with WP nodes inside gets one badge with the worst issue, so you don't have to open it. The Validation strictness setting decides what both show: everything (Strict), no blue info notes (Relaxed), or nothing (Permissive).
- In WP Debug, after a run. The Warnings tab lists what came up during the run, one line each.
Figure: The Starter scene combine reads $mood, which nothing sets, so its row shows MISSING VAR. The run still goes ahead. Screenshot of a WP Context (modules 3 / 3) wired into a WP Prompt Assembler. The Context holds Starter subject, Starter scene and Starter style; the Starter scene combine row is outlined in amber with a MISSING VAR badge, because it reads $mood and nothing upstream sets it. The Assembler's template is '$scene, $style, masterpiece, highly detailed' and the preview still resolves to 'wolf, oil painting, masterpiece, highly detailed'. Warnings are advisory; the run carries on.

sections.title: What the colours mean
sections.text:
- Blue: for your information, usually nothing to fix.
- Amber: worth a look; something probably isn't doing what you meant.
- Red: something points nowhere, such as a reference to a deleted wildcard. The run still finishes; that piece just does nothing.
None of these ever stops a run. Setting a variable twice is fine, for example; the later one wins and the dot just shows it.

sections.title: Common things it flags
sections.text:
Shadowed variable
An earlier WP Context already sets this variable and this one replaces it. Normal when you chain Contexts; shown in blue so you know it's happening.
Duplicate variable
Two modules on the same Context set the same variable, and the lower one wins. Rename one, or reorder them if the wrong value comes through.
Missing variable
The Assembler template uses a $variable nothing sets (or a hidden one), so it prints nothing. The token is underlined in the template. Add a module that sets it, or remove the token.
Constraint can't reach
A constraint can't find one of its wildcards, or they're in the wrong order. It must sit after the source wildcard and before the target.
Constraint never applied
The constraint's target never ran after it, so it changed nothing. Often fine; it's just telling you.
The full list is on Warning & conflict types.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: Warning & conflict types WP Debug Constraints in depth

pages.title: WP Context
pages.blurb: Holds your modules, rolls them every run and passes the $variables on.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
Add a wildcard and the node rolls it into $subject; add a fixed value and you get $style. On every Generate the node runs its modules from top to bottom and passes the finished list of variables to the next node.
Good for
- One per pack or per character
- A second, chained Context that adds to or replaces the first
Better with something else
- Text typed onto the canvas or an LLM caption: use WP Context Injector
Figure: A WP Context with a few modules, wired into the next node. Screenshot of a WP Context (seed 42, fixed, modules 4 / 4) wired into a WP Debug. The Context holds four wildcard rows: Starter subject ($subject), Hair ($hair), Pose ($pose) and Weather ($weather), each with 4 options and the lock, globe and bin buttons on the right, with Add module and Add Bundle at the bottom. The Debug's Variables tab (seed 42, 4 steps, clean run) lists $subject tiger (tag feline), $hair black hair (tag cool), $pose standing and $weather golden hour (tag dry), each with the module that set it.

sections.title: Use it
sections.text:
- Click Add module and pick from your library, or Add Bundle for a saved group.
- Mind the order: modules run top to bottom. A combine that reads $mood goes below the wildcard that picks it, and a constraint goes between its two wildcards.
- Wire context into a WP Prompt Assembler and write a template such as a photo of $subject.
Drag a row by its handle to reorder it or move it to another Context. Untick a row to switch it off. Right-click a row for Edit, Duplicate, Hold across run, Save to library and more.

sections.title: Inputs and outputs
sections.text:
upstream (in)
Optional. Another WP Context, an Injector, Model Info or a Loop. This node starts with their variables and can add to them or replace them.
seed
Decides every random pick in this node. See Seeds & loops.
context (out)
The variables. Wire it into a WP Prompt Assembler, a WP Debug or another WP Context.

sections.title: What the row markers mean
sections.text:
Coloured dot or label
Something to look at, such as MISSING VAR or a variable set twice. Blue is for your information, amber is worth a look. Hover for the message. Nothing here stops a run.
drift
The library entry changed after you added it. Right-click → Refresh from library to take the change. On a bundle it reads library updated; right-click the bundle → Reset to library snapshot.
missing
The entry isn't in your library (deleted, or the workflow came from someone else). The row still works from its own copy; right-click → Save to library to add it.
mod
You changed this row on the node, so it differs from the library.
held
Hold across run is on.
Lock / globe / bin
The row buttons: lock the pick, hide the variable from the prompt, remove the row. Set Row buttons to On hover (ComfyUI Settings or the Display Playground) to show them only when the pointer is on the row; a pressed lock or globe always shows.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
- Chaining: a later Context can set the same variable again, and the later value wins. See Context chaining.
- Keep a pick steady: Lock pick / Lock seed keeps it for good, Hold across run for one Generate. See Seeds & loops.
- Duplicate renames the copy's variable ($hair becomes $hair_2) so the copy rolls on its own.
- Rows are copies. Editing a module in the library doesn't change the workflow until you Refresh the row, so a saved workflow keeps giving the same results.
Where @{} references look
A reference such as @{color} looks for its wildcard among this node's rows first (even a switched-off row), then in the library of the machine that runs the workflow. Keep the wildcards a reference needs on the node and a workflow you share works on someone else's machine too. WP Debug shows where each pick came from.
Wire a WP Debug to the output to see exactly what each module picked.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Prompt Assembler WP Context Loop Per-iteration overrides WP Context Injector Wildcard Constraint

pages.title: WP Context Loop
pages.blurb: Make several variations in one Generate.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
Set the count to 8, press Generate once, and you get eight prompts (and eight images from your sampler), each with its own picks. No queueing the same workflow by hand.
Good for
- A batch of variations from one click
- A story told over several frames
- Comparing chosen options side by side (Sweep)
Better with something else
- Just giving the sampler a new seed per frame: add WP Seed List
Figure: WP Context Loop (count 4) → WP Context → WP Prompt Assembler using $iteration of $iteration_total → one prompt per frame. Screenshot of a four-node loop chain. A WP Context Loop (seed 42, fixed, count 4, strategy hash, Edit frame chips base and #1 to #4, iteration var $iteration) feeds a WP Context holding Starter subject and Starter style, which feeds a WP Prompt Assembler with the template '$iteration of $iteration_total: a picture of a $subject, in the style of $style' and chips $iteration, $iteration_total, $subject and $style. A Preview as Text node shows the run's prompts, starting '1 of 4: a picture of a wolf, in the style of oil painting' and '2 of 4: a picture of a dog, in the style of oil painting'. One prompt per frame.

sections.title: Set it up
sections.text:
- Add WP Context Loop and wire its context output into your first WP Context's upstream.
- Set count.
- Optional: add a WP Seed List on loop_config so each image also gets its own sampler seed.
Without a Seed List, a plain KSampler uses one seed for every frame. Two frames that roll the same prompt then give the same image.

sections.title: The controls
sections.text:
seed
The loop's own seed. Only used when Override Context seed is on.
count
How many frames one Generate makes (1–999). 1 switches looping off without unwiring the node.
values
Optional text from another node: one frame per line (or per list entry), each writing its line to $iteration_value. The values set the frame count and count follows the last run; with a sweep on, every value runs every combination. Its dot sits beside the iteration variable (beside the values note once wired) and shows when you hover it.
Strategy
hash, sequential or stride: how the frame seeds are worked out when Override Context seed is on. See Seeds & loops.
Per-iteration seeds
The seed each frame will use. Lock single frames, Lock all, Copy / Paste, or Prev to keep the seed a frame used last run. Locks need Override Context seed on.
Sweep combinations
Run every combination of the options you pick instead of random rolls. See below.
Edit frame
The base / #1 #2 … chips. Pick a frame to change just that frame (see Per-iteration overrides). Ctrl-click skips a frame, Alt-click locks its seed.
Override Context seed
On: the loop sets every frame's seed from its own seed, so the batch can be repeated. Off (default): each WP Context keeps its own seed and the loop changes it a little per frame.
Iteration var
The name of the frame-number variable ($iteration). The globe and Σ buttons hide or show $iteration and $iteration_total in the prompt.
Bypass loop
Runs a single frame while the node stays wired.

sections.title: Sweep combinations
sections.text:
Instead of random rolls, run every combination of the options you choose. Open Sweep combinations, switch it on and add wildcards from the WP Contexts after the loop. Sweep $hair (3 options) against $mood (2 options) and one Generate makes 6 frames: red + calm, red + sad, blue + calm, and so on. The window shows the total and lists every frame before you run.
Figure: The Sweep window: $subject (4 options) × $hair (4 options) = 16 combinations, each listed as a frame. Screenshot of the WP Context Loop Sweep window ('Run every combination of the wildcards you pick, one frame each'). Sweep combinations is on and reads 4 × 4 = 16 combinations. Two swept wildcards are listed: $subject (4/4, its options cat, tiger, dog and wolf all ticked, with all / none / enabled only links) and $hair (4/4). Limit is 64 and Hold other picks is on. The Frames list shows #1 cat · strawberry blonde hair through #16 wolf · black hair, the first wildcard changing slowest. Behind the window the loop node shows 16 frame chips and a 16 FRAMES badge on Sweep combinations.
all / none / enabled only
Quick ways to tick a wildcard's options. A wildcard with nothing ticked isn't swept.
Order
The first wildcard changes slowest, so two wildcards read like a grid. Use the arrows to reorder.
Limit
The most frames a sweep runs (64 by default, up to 999). Past it, the first combinations run and the window says so.
Hold other picks
On by default: everything you aren't sweeping keeps one pick on every frame, so only the swept part changes.
Keep the sampler on one fixed seed for a clean comparison, so the image only changes where the prompt does.
How it works
A swept wildcard's pick is set by the sweep, so constraints don't change its odds. That means sweeping a constraint's target can show pairs your pack normally rules out. Constraints it drives still apply to the wildcards after it, and its tags still roll.
Skipped frames and seed locks move with their combination when you change the sweep, and are dropped when that combination no longer runs.

sections.title: Frame numbers in the prompt
sections.text:
$iteration is the frame number (from 1) and $iteration_total the count. A template of frame $iteration of $iteration_total, $subject gives "frame 1 of 4, a fox", "frame 2 of 4, a cat" and so on. Both are hidden from the prompt until you switch off the globe and Σ buttons; while hidden you can still use them in derivation rules.
Figure: A full looped workflow: the loop's loop_config feeds a WP Seed List on the sampler, so each of the four frames gets its own prompt and its own seed. Screenshot of a full looped workflow and its output. Top row: WP Context Loop (seed 42, fixed, count 4, hash, with Per-iteration seeds and Sweep combinations rows and Edit frame chips base and #1 to #4) feeds a WP Context holding Starter subject and Starter style, which feeds a WP Prompt Assembler with the template 'iteration $iteration of $iteration_total: a picture of a $subject, in the style of $style'. A Preview as Text node lists the four prompts: a dog, a cat, a dog and a wolf, each in the style of oil painting. Bottom row: Load Checkpoint, a WP Seed List fed by the loop's loop_config whose seed goes to the KSampler, two CLIP Text Encode nodes (prompt and negative from the Assembler), Empty Latent Image, VAE Decode and a Preview Image showing a 2 by 2 grid of painted animal portraits captioned iteration 1 of 4 to iteration 4 of 4: a dog, a cat, a dog and a wolf. One image per frame, each with its own prompt and seed.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
- A module on Lock pick / Lock seed keeps its pick on every frame. Hold across run keeps it for one Generate. See Seeds & loops.
- Per-frame changes stay on the canvas: bundles don't save them and the Test Runner doesn't run them.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: Seeds & loops Per-iteration overrides WP Seed List WP Context WP Prompt Assembler

pages.title: WP Seed List
pages.blurb: One sampler seed per loop frame, so each frame makes its own image.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A plain KSampler takes one seed and uses it for every frame of a loop. Two frames that roll the same prompt then make the same image. WP Seed List gives the sampler a list of seeds instead, one per frame: frame 1 gets seed 1, frame 2 gets seed 2, and so on.
Good for
- Giving each loop frame its own sampler seed
- Keeping an image you liked reproducible (lock its seed)
Better with something else
- Prompt variety: it never changes a prompt. The Context seed and the Loop do that

sections.title: Set it up
sections.text:
Figure: Wire the loop's loop_config into the Seed List and its seed output into the sampler's seed. Steps: WP Context Loop (N prompts) → loop_config → WP Seed List (N seeds) → paired in order → KSampler (N different images). Flow diagram of three nodes left to right: WP Context Loop (N prompts), an arrow labelled loop_config, WP Seed List (N seeds), an arrow labelled paired in order, and KSampler (N different images). Caption: wire the loop's loop_config into the Seed List and its seed output into the sampler's seed.
- Wire the loop's loop_config output into the Seed List.
- Wire the Seed List's seed output into your sampler's seed input (right-click the sampler and convert seed to an input if needed).
The count now follows the loop, so the two lists always line up.
Figure: WP Context Loop's loop_config wired into WP Seed List, whose seed output drives the KSampler's seed. Screenshot of three nodes. A WP Context Loop (seed 42, fixed, count 4, strategy hash) has its loop_config output wired into a WP Seed List. The Seed List shows base_seed 0, a greyed count (taken from the loop), strategy hash, a Per-iteration seeds button, seed chips #1 to #4 ('Click a frame to lock its seed'), Override base seed from loop off, and Override count from loop and Override strategy from loop on. Its seed output is wired into the seed input of a KSampler.

sections.title: The controls
sections.text:
base_seed
Where the seed list starts. Same base, same seeds.
count
How many seeds it gives (1–999). Follows the loop's count while Override count from loop is on.
Strategy
hash, sequential (base, base+1 …) or stride. It changes which numbers you get, not how varied the images are.
Per-iteration seeds
Lock single seeds, Lock all, Copy / Paste, or Prev to keep the seed a frame used last run.
Override … from loop
Three switches: take the base seed, the count and the strategy from the wired loop. Count and strategy switch on by themselves when you connect loop_config; base seed stays yours unless you switch it on.
Prev is the one to use after a run you liked: the list shows the seeds for the next run, and Prev locks the seed the frame actually used.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
- Without a loop it still gives count seeds, so the sampler runs that many times. Set count to 1 for a single seed.
- Unplugging loop_config leaves the switches as they were; the node falls back to its own values.
- Seeds stay in the range ComfyUI's own randomize button uses, so you can copy one into a plain sampler and get the same image.
- More on seeds: Seeds & loops.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: Seeds & loops WP Context Loop Per-iteration overrides WP Context

pages.title: WP Context Injector
pages.blurb: Turn any value on the canvas into a $variable.

sections.title: An example
sections.text:
You have a text box with red hoodie, ripped jeans and another with rooftop at night. Wire both into an Injector, name the rows $outfit and $place, and a template of a woman wearing $outfit, $place prints "a woman wearing red hoodie, ripped jeans, rooftop at night".
Figure: Two text boxes wired into a WP Context Injector, named $outfit and $place, used in the Assembler's template. Screenshot of outside text becoming variables. Two Text (Multiline) nodes, 'red hoodie, ripped jeans, sneakers' and 'rooftop at night, neon signs, light rain', wire into input_0 and input_1 of a WP Context Injector. Its injected variables list (2 / 2) shows two string rows named outfit and place. The Injector's context feeds a WP Prompt Assembler with the template 'a woman wearing $outfit, $place, cinematic' and chips $outfit and $place, and a Preview as Text node prints the run's result: 'a woman wearing red hoodie, ripped jeans, sneakers, rooftop at night, neon signs, light rain, cinematic'.
Good for
- Text from outside your library: something you type, an LLM caption, a LoRA name
- A number from a slider or another node
Better with something else
- Choices: an injected value isn't a pick, so nothing can constrain it. Use a wildcard with Match variable
- Reusable text that rolls: a Combine in the library

sections.title: Use it
sections.text:
- Wire any output into the next free input_N. A row appears for it.
- Type the variable's name in the row.
- Wire context into a WP Context, an Assembler or a Debug. Wire an existing Context into upstream to add to it; its variables pass through.
Figure: The Injector gives an outside value a name the rest of the workflow can use. Steps: Any node (any output) → wire → WP Context Injector (names it $var) → $variable → WP Context (merged in). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: Any node (any output), an arrow labelled wire, WP Context Injector (names it $var), an arrow labelled $variable, and WP Context (merged in). Caption: the Injector gives an outside value a name the rest of the workflow can use.

sections.title: Row options
sections.text:
Right-click a row → Edit for its template and negative.
Name
The $variable the value becomes. Letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter.
Template
Optional. Wrap the value in text, e.g. wearing $input_0. Leave empty to use the value as it is. $$ prints a dollar sign.
Negative
Optional negative words for this variable (it can use $input_0 too, so another node can write it). Only reaches an Assembler that prints the variable. Rows with one show a NEG badge.
Hide from prompt (globe)
The variable still reaches combines and derivations, but prints nothing in the prompt.

sections.title: Join several inputs
sections.text:
Click Add template row and write a template like $input_0 by $input_1. A template row isn't tied to one input, stays when you rewire, and runs after the other rows, so it can also use the variables they made ($outfit).
How it works
A row made for a wired input can only use its own input in its template. It disappears when you unplug that input. Up to 10 inputs per Injector; chain a second one for more. Text works best: images and latents turn into their text description, which is rarely useful in a prompt.
Setting a variable here clears the negatives it had from earlier nodes; the row's own negative takes their place. A hidden row, or one that only feeds a derivation, never adds to a negative.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Context WP Prompt Assembler Negatives

pages.title: WP Model Info
pages.blurb: Name the loaded checkpoint so rules can branch on it.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
One prompt setup rarely suits every checkpoint. Pony wants its score tags, Illustrious wants different LoRAs, Flux reads plain sentences. WP Model Info looks at the model you loaded and writes what it found into the Context, so the rest of the pipeline can react to it.
$model_family
The architecture, read from the loaded model itself: sd15, sdxl, flux, sd3, chroma and so on. Needs the model input.
$model_variant
The fine-tune line, read from the checkpoint's file name by the variant rules: pony, illustrious, noobai, animagine, or empty when no rule matches.
$model_name
The checkpoint's file name without folders or extension, e.g. ponyDiffusionV6XL.
Pony and Illustrious are both SDXL underneath, so $model_family reads sdxl for both. $model_variant tells them apart, and it can only come from the file name.
Some models read in ways you might not expect:
Flux.1 and Flux.2
Both read as flux.
Anima
Probably reads as cosmos.
Z-Image
Probably reads as lumina2.
Models with no entry
Krea 2, Kolors and others read as their class name, in lower case with underscores.
Merges
A file name without "noob", "pony" or "illustrious" in it gets no variant.
Check once what the node reads for your checkpoint, then pin the variant or add a rule for its file name. Notes per model are on Writing prompts for your model.
Good for
- One pack that writes different quality tags, LoRAs or styles per checkpoint
Better with something else
- A workflow that only ever runs one model: a fixed value is simpler

sections.title: Where it goes
sections.text:
Figure: Model Info heads the chain, so every Context after it can read the model variables. Steps: Load Checkpoint (MODEL) → model → WP Model Info ($model_variant) → context → WP Context (rules branch on it). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: Load Checkpoint (MODEL), an arrow labelled MODEL, WP Model Info ($model_variant), an arrow labelled context, and WP Context (rules branch on it). Caption: Model Info heads the chain, so every Context after it can read the model variables.
If a node that loads LoRAs from the prompt sits on the model, wire Model Info to the MODEL from before that node. Otherwise the prompt needs the model and the model needs the prompt, and ComfyUI refuses to run the loop.
Figure: Load Checkpoint → WP Model Info → WP Context → Assembler. The family is pinned to sdxl, the variant is read from the file name, and the template prints both. Screenshot of four nodes. Load Checkpoint (waiIllustriousSDXL_v150.safetensors) sends MODEL into the model input of WP Model Info. Its Detected section lists family sdxl (pinned), variant illustrious (from a rule) and name waiIllustriousSDXL_v150 (from the loader), each with globe and pin buttons; Variant rules map noobai → noob, pony → pony|pdxl, illustrious → illustrious|ilxl (matched) and animagine → animagine. Its context feeds a WP Context with Starter subject, then a WP Prompt Assembler with the template '$subject, $model_family style, $model_variant' and the preview 'wolf, sdxl style, illustrious'.

sections.title: Inputs, outputs and controls
sections.text:
upstream (in)
An existing Context to extend. Only nodes after Model Info see its variables, so it usually goes first.
model (in)
The MODEL from your checkpoint loader. Gives the family, and the node follows the wire back to the loader for the file name, stepping over LoRA loaders and other model patches.
family, variant, name (in)
Optional text from another node, such as a switch that names the model you're testing. A wired value beats the pin and detection (an empty one is ignored); a wired name goes through the variant rules like the loader's. The row shows wired, and its value after a run. Each input's dot sits beside its row, like a built-in widget's, and shows when you hover the row or wire it.
Detected
The three values and where each comes from. Variant and name update as soon as you change the loader's checkpoint; the family shows after the first run.
Globe
Whether the variable can print. All three start hidden: rules and constraints read them, but the Assembler leaves them out. Click the globe to print one.
Pin
Use your own value for a row instead of the detected one: a file name when no model is wired, or a variant to try your Pony rules without switching checkpoint. Click it again to go back to detection.
Variant rules
Rows of variant and pattern. The first pattern found in the file name sets $model_variant, and its row lights up. Capitals don't matter; | separates alternatives (pony|pdxl). A broken row is outlined in red and skipped. Reset brings back the built-in rules.
context (out)
The upstream Context plus the three variables.

sections.title: LoRAs per model
sections.text: In the derivation editor, LoRA by model adds a ready-made rule: if $model_variant is pony, set $loras to a Pony LoRA tag; if illustrious, an Illustrious one; otherwise leave it empty. Swap the placeholder LoRA names for yours, add branches for other variants, and put $loras in your Assembler template. The same pattern works for quality tags, negatives or anything else a derivation can write.

sections.title: Constraints from the model
sections.text:
Constraints react to a wildcard's pick, not to a variable, so the model reaches them through a wildcard. Make a wildcard (say Model) with options pony and illustrious, tag them, add it to your Context, and in its node settings set Match variable to model_variant. Instead of rolling, it picks the option whose text equals the detected variant, and any constraint can use it as its source, for example “if Model is pony, exclude photo styles”.
Mark one option of that wildcard as the fallback (for example “other”), so checkpoints your rules don't recognise still get a predictable pick. Without a fallback the wildcard rolls as usual and WP Debug notes that nothing matched.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
The canvas previews $model_variant and $model_name from the loader's file name straight away. $model_family needs the loaded model, so it previews as a placeholder until the first run (or pin it).
Model Info lives in the workflow, not your library, so packs that branch on $model_variant work on any version that has the node.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Context Derivation Constraint WP Context Injector

pages.title: WP Toggles
pages.blurb: Several on/off switches in one node, as $variables and BOOLEAN outputs, that can also mute or bypass nodes.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
WP Toggles replaces a stack of Boolean nodes. Each toggle writes $its_variable as true or false, so a derivation can branch on it without a Context Injector, and can show a BOOLEAN output at the right of its row for a switch node.
Figure: LoRA character is off, so the LoRA wired into its dot is bypassed and Use its own clothes (which needs it) is off too. A WP Toggles node in its clean view (a pencil at the top opens the edit view). Rows: LoRA character (a switch, off, $use_lora_character, with a violet bypass icon by its name), whose dot on the left is wired from a Load LoRA node shown bypassed in purple; Use its own clothes (indented, striped, 'Off: needs LoRA character'); Anime look (a chip); then a Scene label with Time of day (Day / Night buttons, $is_day), whose BOOLEAN dot at the right edge is wired to a Preview as Text node.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- Switches you flip by hand: use a LoRA, add a detailer, day or night
- Paths a rule picks between: $use_lora_character in a derivation
Better with something else
- A switch a random pick should flip: a wildcard and WP Var → Bool

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
upstream (in)
Optional Context to extend. Only nodes after this one see the toggle variables. It can also set toggles (see below).
Pencil (top)
Opens the edit view: the mode, the grips to reorder, a pencil per row, Add toggle and Add label. Done goes back to the clean view, which shows only the switches.
Any on / Pick one
Any on: every toggle is on or off by itself. Pick one: exactly one is on, like radio buttons.
writes (Pick one)
Optional variable that also gets the picked toggle's value (or its name), so one rule can branch on it.
Pencil (row)
Opens the toggle's edit panel: name, variable, style, needs, what off mutes or bypasses, group and its output.
Add toggle / Add label
A new toggle, or a label that groups the toggles under it. Click a label's arrow to fold it.
control dots (in)
A toggle that mutes or bypasses has a dot at the left of its row: wire the nodes it drives into it.
context (out)
The Context with every toggle variable added, all internal.
toggle outputs
One BOOLEAN per toggle that has an output, at the right of its row. Up to 16.

sections.title: Editing a toggle
sections.text:
Name
Shown on the row and on its output.
Variable
Gets true or false. It follows the name until you change it. Always internal, so it never prints in the prompt. Show puts it under the name in the clean view.
Style
Switch, Check, Buttons (two words of your own, like Day / Night) or Chip (a small chip with the name).
Value (Pick one)
What the picked variable gets when this toggle is picked, instead of its name. It can read $variables from upstream.
Needs
Another toggle this one needs. While that one is off, this one is off too; it keeps your choice for when it comes back on.
When off
Nothing, Mute or Bypass: what happens to the nodes wired into the row's dot (and to the canvas groups you pick) while the toggle is off. On, they run.
Invert
Mute or bypass while the toggle is ON instead, for a node used only as a switchboard.
Canvas groups
Groups on the canvas whose nodes When off also covers, by title. No wires needed.
Upstream can set it
When the upstream Context holds this toggle's variable as a yes/no word (true, yes, on, 1, false, no, off, 0), that value sets the switch for the run.
Group
Which label it sits under.
BOOLEAN output
Show an output for switch nodes. Off for a toggle only rules read.
Drag the grip to reorder. A label moves with its toggles. Moving a row never re-points a wire: each output stays with its toggle.

sections.title: Mute or bypass nodes
sections.text:
Set a toggle's When off to Mute or Bypass and its row gets a dot on the left. Wire any node's output into it, or a WP Node Group to drive several. Turning the toggle off mutes or bypasses them; turning it on lets them run. Needs and Pick one count: a toggle that is off because of them drives its nodes off too. A toggle can do all of it at once: write $its_variable, send its BOOLEAN and mute or bypass. Once something is wired, an icon next to the name shows it: coloured while it is muting or bypassing, dim while not; hover it for the nodes.
Figure: Detailer is off, so the two nodes in its WP Node Group are muted. Two nodes, Detailer decode and Detail upscale, are wired into a WP Node Group, which lists them as muted rows with Run / Mute / Bypass buttons at the top. Its nodes output is wired into the dot at the left of the Detailer row of a WP Toggles node; Detailer is set to Off and shows a mute icon by its name.
This happens on the canvas, the moment the toggle flips, so the saved workflow keeps the modes. The wires to the dots never reach the run. An upstream value that sets a toggle changes its variable and output, not the modes.

sections.title: Pick one
sections.text: One toggle is on. Which one, first match wins: the toggle the upstream picked variable names (with Upstream can pick), then the first toggle upstream set to a yes word, then the first one you switched on. The picked variable gets the toggle's Value, or its name; it is internal unless Show in prompt is on.

sections.title: Merge the Boolean nodes you have
sections.text: Select Boolean nodes, right-click one and pick Merge into WP Toggles. Each becomes a toggle named after its title, keeps its value, and its wires move to the matching output. A node can merge when its only output is BOOLEAN, nothing is wired into it and it has one on/off value, so ComfyUI's Boolean and most pack toggles work. Ctrl+Z undoes the merge.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Context Injector WP Var → Bool WP Node Group WP Mode Relay WP Model Info

pages.title: WP Node Group
pages.blurb: Gather nodes so one WP Toggles switch mutes or bypasses them all.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
WP Node Group collects nodes for a WP Toggles control. Wire the nodes in on the left and its output into a toggle's dot: when the toggle is off, every node in the group is muted or bypassed. Groups can go into groups. It never runs and is left out of the prompt.
Figure: Two nodes in a group, wired into Detailer's dot. Detailer is off, so both are muted. Two nodes, Detailer decode and Detail upscale, are wired into a WP Node Group, which lists them as muted rows with Run / Mute / Bypass buttons at the top. Its nodes output is wired into the dot at the left of the Detailer row of a WP Toggles node; Detailer is set to Off and shows a mute icon by its name.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- One switch for a whole branch: a detailer, an upscale pass, a LoRA stack
- Muting or bypassing by hand from one place
Better with something else
- Nodes that already sit in one canvas group: pick the group in the toggle instead

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
node dots (in)
Wire any node's output in. A new free dot appears as you wire; a freed one goes. Each shows its node's title.
nodes (out)
Wire it into a WP Toggles control dot: that toggle then mutes or bypasses every node here.
Run / Mute / Bypass
Set every node in the group at once.
Mode chip
Each row's chip shows its node's mode. Click it to go Runs → Muted → Bypassed.
Muting or bypassing the group node itself does the same to its nodes, and setting it back lets them run.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Toggles WP Mode Relay

pages.title: WP Mode Relay
pages.blurb: When the nodes it watches get muted or bypassed, mute, bypass or run a WP Node Group.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
WP Mode Relay chains mutes and bypasses. It watches the nodes wired into it and, when what they do changes, sets the nodes of the WP Node Group its output goes into. So muting a sampler can bypass its whole save branch, or bypassing one LoRA can let a different one run. It never runs and is left out of the prompt.
Figure: The watched node is muted, so the relay mutes the node in its WP Node Group. A node titled Watched is muted and wired into a WP Mode Relay, whose table maps All muted to Mute (highlighted as the current case), All bypassed to Bypass and Any runs to Run, with the line 'Watching 1 node: muted · drives 1 node'. The relay's drives output goes into a WP Node Group whose one member, Follower, is shown muted.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- Turning one branch off when another is off
- Swapping: bypass A when B runs
Better with something else
- One switch for several nodes: a WP Toggles row with a WP Node Group

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
watch dots (in)
Wire the nodes to watch. A new free dot appears as you wire.
drives (out)
Wire it into a WP Node Group: the relay sets that group's nodes.
All muted
What to send when every watched node is muted: Run, Mute, Bypass or nothing (—).
All bypassed
What to send when every watched node is bypassed.
Any runs
What to send when at least one watched node runs.
A mix of muted and bypassed sends nothing. The relay acts only when the watched nodes change, never when a workflow loads.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Node Group WP Toggles

pages.title: WP Bookmark
pages.blurb: Mark a spot on the canvas and jump back to it with a shortcut or from the Bookmarks dock.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
WP Bookmark marks a place in a big workflow. Press its shortcut, or click it in the Bookmarks dock, and the canvas glides there: the bookmark lands at the corner, edge or centre of the screen you picked, at the zoom you picked. It never runs and is left out of the prompt; its settings are saved with the workflow.
Figure: Sampler in its one-line read view; Prompts open in the editor, where the clash check flags Ctrl+S. Screenshot of a small text-to-image graph (Positive prompt, Negative prompt and Empty Latent Image into a KSampler, then VAE Decode) with two WP Bookmark nodes. On the right, Sampler (amber title bar) shows its read view: one line with a lightning icon, Centre · 1.25×, the shortcut Alt + 1, a Go button and a pencil to edit. On the left, Prompts (green title bar) is open in its editor: a pencil icon, colour #22c55e, the name and Go; Lands at shows a 3 × 3 grid with the top-left dot picked (Top left of the screen, 24 px in); Zoom is set to Keep current; the shortcut is Ctrl + S with a lightning (suggest) and × (clear) button, under which an amber warning reads Also Save Workflow (ComfyUI); Show on canvas is on, and Done closes the editor.

sections.title: Notes as bookmarks
sections.text: A WP Note can be a bookmark too: turn on Also a bookmark in its editor. It gets the same Lands at, Zoom and Shortcut settings and shows in the dock in the note's colour, but it never hides on the canvas, and muting it turns its shortcut off without fading it.

sections.title: Read view and editor
sections.text: A saved bookmark shows one line: its icon, where it lands and its zoom, its shortcut (with a warning mark when something else uses it), Go and a pencil. The pencil, or a double-click on the node, opens the editor; Done closes it. A new bookmark opens in the editor.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- Jumping between the prompt, the sampler and the outputs of a large graph
- A tour of a shared workflow: step through it with Next
- Getting back to the same view and zoom every time
Better with something else
- Explaining a step to someone: a WP Note

sections.title: Settings
sections.text:
Icon, colour, name
How the bookmark shows in the dock. The colour also tints the node's title bar.
Go
Jump now.
Lands at
A 3×3 grid: the corner, edge or centre of the screen the bookmark goes to, 24 px in from the edge (beside the dock while it's open).
Zoom
Set jumps to that zoom (0.1–10×; the magnifier takes the zoom you're at). Keep current leaves it alone.
Shortcut
Record, then press the keys (Esc cancels, Backspace clears). The bolt picks a free one.
Show on canvas
Off hides the node: not drawn, not clickable, not selectable. The dock's eye shows it again.
Muting or bypassing a bookmark turns it off: its shortcut does nothing and the dock greys it.

sections.title: Shortcut clashes
sections.text:
While you set a shortcut, the node lists who else uses it.
Refused
Keys the browser keeps: Ctrl+T, Ctrl+W, Ctrl+1–9, F5, F11 and the like.
Warning
A ComfyUI shortcut (yours from Settings › Keybinding included), another extension's, another WP Bookmark's, or an rgthree bookmark's in the same workflow.
Note
No Ctrl or Alt: it fires whenever the canvas has focus, never while you type.
Extensions that read keys themselves can't be seen in advance. If one takes the key first, the bookmark doesn't jump and a toast names the combo once, so you can pick another.

sections.title: The Bookmarks dock
sections.text:
The bookmark button in the top bar shows or hides the dock. It also opens by itself in a workflow with bookmarks, unless you closed it.
Figure: The dock in view mode: click a row to jump. Its pencil opens edit mode, where the eye brings back a hidden bookmark. Screenshot of the Bookmarks dock, in view mode, at the top left of the canvas. Its header reads Bookmarks, 4 · 1 hidden, with Back, Previous, Next, a pencil to edit and Close. The rows show a number, a coloured icon, a name and a shortcut: 1 Prompts (Alt + 1), 2 Sampler (Alt + 2, highlighted as the bookmark just jumped to), 3 Upscale in grey italics with a small crossed-out eye because it is hidden on the canvas (Alt + 3), and 4 Save and share marked OFF because the node is muted. To the right of the dock the canvas shows the Sampler bookmark in its one-line read view (Top left · 1×, Alt + 2, Go, pencil), landed at the top left beside the dock, then the KSampler, VAE Decode and the muted Save and share bookmark (greyed, marked OFF), with the prompt and latent nodes below; the hidden Upscale bookmark is not drawn.
Row
Click to jump. Number, icon, name and shortcut; a mark for one hidden on the canvas or inside a subgraph, OFF for a muted one.
Back
Return to where you were before the last jump.
↑ / ↓
Step through the bookmarks that are on, in dock order.
Pencil
Edit mode: drag the grips to reorder, the eye shows or hides a bookmark on the canvas, the arrow moves the dock to the other side, and Bookmark this view adds one at the top-left of the screen with the zoom you're at. Done goes back.
Next, Previous, Back, Bookmark this view and the dock toggle are commands without keys: bind them in Settings › Keybinding.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Note WP Node Group WP Toggles

pages.title: WP Prompt Assembler
pages.blurb: Write a template with $variables and get the prompt and its negative.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
Write a $style portrait of $subject, $lighting and the Assembler puts each variable's value in its place, every run. The result is plain text for CLIP Text Encode. Variables you set to Hide from prompt print nothing.
Good for
- One per prompt you need: the main prompt, a face detailer, one per region
- Each reads the same Context, so their picks agree
Better with something else
- Rolling anything: it has no seed. Pick in a wildcard and use its $variable
Figure: The Assembler with a template, its variable chips and the resolved preview. A variable nothing sets is underlined and shown as a dashed chip. Screenshot of a WP Context (Starter subject, Hair, Pose) wired into a WP Prompt Assembler. The template reads 'photo of a $subject with $hair, $pose, $mood lighting, masterpiece', with $mood underlined in red because nothing upstream sets it. The variables header reads 3 upstream · 1 missing; the chips are $subject, $hair and $pose, then a dashed amber 'mood' chip with a warning icon. The preview reads 'photo of a wolf with black hair, standing, $mood lighting, masterpiece', leaving the missing variable visible.

sections.title: Write a template
sections.text:
- Type $ and pick a variable, or click a chip in the variables strip to insert it at the cursor.
- A variable nothing sets is underlined in amber and shows as a dashed chip, and prints nothing when you run. Click the chip to remove it from the template.
- $$ prints a single dollar sign.
- Save and Load in the toolbar keep templates in your library (see Templates).
The Assembler doesn't roll. {a|b|c} prints exactly as typed and @{…} prints nothing. Put choices in a wildcard or combine and print its variable.
How empty variables are tidied
When a variable comes out empty, the commas around it and a joining word left with nothing after it ("with", "and") are removed. Your own words stay: with $hat, $scarf and $place empty, a girl wearing $hat with $scarf, $pose, in the $place gives "a girl wearing, sitting". Write templates that still read well when something is empty (put the verb inside a combine), and use WP Prompt Cleaner to remove duplicates. Emoticon tags such as :d are kept.

sections.title: The negative output
sections.text:
Wildcard options, fixed values, combines and derivations can carry negative words. The negative output collects them, but only for variables this template printed: an Assembler for a face detailer that prints just $face never gets the hair negatives.
Figure: Hair, Weather and Quality feed an Assembler with both outputs wired. The negative preview shows the words collected from the variables the template printed. Screenshot of a WP Context (seed 3) holding Hair, Weather and Quality, wired into a WP Prompt Assembler whose prompt and negative outputs each feed a Preview as Text node. The template is '$quality, a woman with $hair, $weather'; the preview reads 'masterpiece, best quality, a woman with black hair, clear sky'. The negative template is empty ('just the variables' negatives'), and the negative preview, marked '1 from variables', reads 'lowres, bad anatomy', which came from the Quality fixed value. The negative Preview as Text prints 'lowres, bad anatomy'.
- Put your standing negative in the negative template, e.g. lowres, bad anatomy, $negatives.
- Leave it empty to output only the collected words. Without $negatives they're added at the end.
- Repeated tags are dropped, also when written with a weight like (blurry:1.2).
- Clear template empties the negative template too.
More in Negatives.

sections.title: Inputs and outputs
sections.text:
context (in)
The variables from a WP Context (or anything that ends in one).
template
Your prompt with $variables in it.
negative_template
Optional, in the collapsible negative section. Your standing negative, with $negatives where the collected negative words go.
prompt (out)
The finished prompt. Wire it into CLIP Text Encode or a WP Prompt Cleaner.
negative (out)
The negative words of the variables this template printed, plus your negative template. Wire it into your negative CLIP Text Encode.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: The $variable pipeline Negatives WP Context WP Prompt Cleaner

pages.title: WP Prompt Cleaner
pages.blurb: Tidy a prompt: duplicates, stray commas, brackets, LoRA tags, blocked words.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Wire a prompt, usually from a WP Prompt Assembler, into the Cleaner. It tidies spaces, empty brackets, stacked weights and LoRA tags, drops duplicate tags, and removes words on your blocklist. The clean text goes on to CLIP Text Encode. It needs no Context.
Good for
- Removing duplicates and near-duplicates after the Assembler
- Merging weights, spacing LoRA tags, blocking words
Better with something else
- Fixing a pack: if it often removes something, fix the option that wrote it
Never blocklist or fuzzy-dedupe a LoRA's trigger words, or the LoRA stops working. The blocklist matches whole words, so list every form of a word you block (see Adult (NSFW) packs). For prose prompts use text mode on Gentle: tags mode splits on commas, so it would split sentences.
Figure: A messy tag list goes into WP Prompt Cleaner and comes out without the doubled tags and stray commas. Each rule shows how many fixes it made. Screenshot of a Text (Multiline) node with a messy prompt ('masterpiece, best quality,, highly detailed, highly detailed, portrait of a young woman , , long flowing red hair, red hair, green eyes,, dramatic lighting , masterpiece') wired into a WP Prompt Cleaner. The Cleaner is in tags mode, intensity balanced; its rules list whitespace 2, punctuation 0, empty groups 0, LoRA spacing 0 and tag dedupe 2, with merge weights, fuzzy dedupe and blocklist off. A Preview as Text node prints 'masterpiece, best quality, highly detailed, portrait of a young woman, long flowing red hair, red hair, green eyes, dramatic lighting'.

sections.title: Inputs and outputs
sections.text:
prompt (in)
The text to clean, usually from a WP Prompt Assembler. Any text works.
cleaner widget
Pick a mode and a preset, switch single rules on or off, and edit the blocklist. After a run it shows how many fixes each rule made.
negative (in)
Optional. A negative to clean too: type it or wire in the Assembler's negative. Left empty, the negative output is empty.
prompt (out)
The cleaned prompt, for CLIP Text Encode.
blocklist (in)
Optional text from another node, such as one shared word list feeding several cleaners. Its entries join the panel's blocklist (comma- or newline-separated in list mode, one per line in regex mode) and turn the blocklist on; the Blocklist button reads + input. Its dot sits beside that button and shows when you hover it or wire it.
negative (out)
The cleaned negative, using the negative column's rules. Wire it into your negative CLIP Text Encode.

sections.title: Mode
sections.text: Tags is for comma-separated tag lists, the usual SD style: the Cleaner works tag by tag. Text is for sentences: tag rules such as duplicate removal are off, and the blocklist removes just the word, not the whole phrase.

sections.title: Presets
sections.text:
Gentle
Only tidies spaces: removes doubled spaces and spaces at the ends. The safest choice.
Balanced
Also removes empty brackets, tidies LoRA tags and stray punctuation, and drops exact duplicate tags. None of these change what the prompt means. A good default.
Aggressive
Also merges stacked weights and drops near-duplicates ("bad hand" and "bad hands"). Now and then it removes something you meant to keep.
Custom
Shown when you've switched single rules away from the preset.

sections.title: Prompt syntax rules
sections.text:
Three rules read brackets and tags the way ComfyUI does. They work in both modes and run first, so anything they leave behind is tidied in the same run.
Empty groups
Removes brackets with nothing inside: (), [], ( , ), (:1.2), and groups left empty once those go. red (), dress becomes red, dress. The usual cause is a weighted reference that printed nothing: (@{hat}:1.2) becomes (:1.2). On from Balanced.
Merge weights
Folds stacked weights into one group by multiplying them, as ComfyUI does (a bare ( ) counts as 1.1): ((a:1.1):1.2) becomes (a:1.32), (((a))) becomes (a:1.33), and (a:1.0) becomes plain a. Only merges when the inner group is everything inside the outer one, rounds to 2 decimals, and never touches [ ]. On in Aggressive.
LoRA spacing
Tidies <lora:…> tags (and lyco, locon, hypernet, <embedding:…>): < lora : x : 0.8 > becomes <lora:x:0.8>, and girl<lora:x:1> becomes girl <lora:x:1>. Spaces inside a file name stay. On from Balanced.
Escaped \( \) stay literal, LoRA and embedding names are never edited, and if the brackets don't balance the bracket rules leave the prompt exactly as written.

sections.title: Cleaning the negative
sections.text:
With a negative wired in, one Cleaner cleans both. The rule list gets a second column of tick boxes for the negative. It follows the prompt column, except near-duplicate removal and the blocklist are off: near-duplicates in a negative are usually on purpose, and blocked words often belong in a negative.
Drop negative tags also in prompt (off by default) removes a tag from the negative when the prompt asks for it too, since the model can't both draw it and avoid it. Either way, the run stats name the tags the two share.

sections.title: Blocklist
sections.text:
Add words or phrases you always want removed. Two modes:
- List: words separated by commas or new lines; capitals don't matter. In Tags mode the whole tag with the word goes; in Text mode just the word.
- Regex: one pattern per line; capitals don't matter. A broken pattern is skipped and named in the run stats.
Hover a rule for what it does. After a run, the count next to each rule shows what it removed.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Prompt Assembler Negatives

pages.title: WP Image Filter
pages.blurb: Pause the run and pick which images (and their prompts) go on.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Upscaling every image of a batch costs time on the ones you'd throw away. Put WP Image Filter between the first KSampler and the upscaler: the run stops there, a picker shows every image, and only the ones you pick continue. Everything that belongs to an image travels with it, so the upscaler gets each picked image's own latent, conditioning and prompt.
Good for
- A human pick before an expensive second pass (hires, upscale, detailer, video)
- Curating a sweep grid
- Inpainting a picked image in the same run
Better with something else
- Unattended runs: the queue waits while the picker is open. Set it to pass all, or give it a timeout

sections.title: Where it goes
sections.text:
Figure: Wire the same conditioning and prompt text through the filter that the upscaler would otherwise take from the start. Steps: KSampler + VAE Decode (images, latent) → images + prompts → WP Image Filter (you pick) → picks → Upscaler (picked only). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: KSampler + VAE Decode (images, latent), an arrow labelled images + prompts, WP Image Filter (you pick), an arrow labelled picks, and Upscaler (picked only). Caption: wire the same conditioning and prompt text through the filter that the upscaler would otherwise take from the start, so only the picked images and their matching data go on.
With a Context Loop, every iteration is a frame. The picker groups images by frame, and the prompt, conditioning and Context of a frame are kept only when one of its images is.

sections.title: Inputs & outputs
sections.text:
Every input has a matching output. Connect only what you need.
images
The images to pick from. Required: this is what the picker shows.
latent, masks
Sliced to the picked images. A mask you paint in the picker replaces that image's mask.
positive, negative
CONDITIONING. A batched conditioning is sliced with the images; a single one is kept for every frame that keeps an image.
positive_text, negative_text
The prompt strings, kept or dropped with their frame.
context
Each frame's WP Context, kept or dropped with it.
clip (in)
Optional. Re-encodes a prompt you edit in the picker, so the positive/negative conditioning follows the edit. Without it, an edit changes only the text outputs.
extra_1, extra_2
Any type. The output takes the type of what you connect. Batched values are sliced, anything else follows its frame.
picks (out)
What was kept, as frame:image (1-based), for example 1:2, 3:1.
labels (out)
One label per item, in step with images: #3 · red · 2 by default, or the name you gave the image in the picker. An item with several images has one line per image.

sections.title: The picker
sections.text:
The picker has three modes, switched at the top or with G, D and Z. The window keeps its size in every mode, the pick count and the Keep buttons stay in the footer, and the picker opens in the mode you left it in.
Figure: Grid: six loop frames of two images each, at tile size M. Three images are picked. Screenshot of the WP Image Filter picker, marked Waiting, in Grid mode (the Grid / Detail / Zoom switch is top right) with Tile size M: 6 frames of 2 images each, every frame a card labelled #1 to #6 with an all button. Three images are picked (green border and tick). The footer reads 3 of 12 picked from 3 frames, with Stop branch, Keep all 12 and Keep 3 picked.
Grid G
Pick fast. Click an image or press Space over it; Ctrl+A picks everything; a frame says how many of its images are picked, and its Pick frame button picks them all. Tile size S, M, L or Fit (F, as big as the picker allows). Double-click an image or click its frame to open it in Detail. Each image's label sits under it; click it to rename.
Detail D
One image next to its size, seed and label (click to rename), with Pick / Picked (P), Compare (C) and Pick frame at the top of the side panel and three tabs under them: Values, Prompt and Mask. Each value is marked in the prompt in its own colour (the same colour in Values); hover a mark to see which variable set it. Prompt and negative have copy buttons. Only what is wired shows. ←/→ step; the strip under the picture groups a loop's images by frame and jumps to any image. C compares two images with a slider, M paints a mask.
Zoom Z
Only the picture, at Fit, 100%, 200% or any level between (− / +, keys 0 1 2). Scroll zooms toward the mouse, drag moves, double-click goes to 100% at that spot. Zoomed in, a mini-map shows where you are (click or drag it to move); the bar fades while the mouse is still. F (or the fullscreen button) fills the screen, with the frame's images and Keep picked along the bottom. ←/→ keep the zoom and the spot on the next image. The label says Picked once picked. C pins the image and the next one shows beside it, locked to the same zoom and spot.
Figure: Zoom on the hand in frame #5 at 200%. The mini-map shows where you are and the label says the image is picked. Step with the arrow keys and the next image opens on the same spot. Screenshot of the WP Image Filter picker in Zoom mode. The picture fills the window, zoomed to 164% on a figure's hand labelled 5 fingers. A bar on top holds ‹, −, Fit, 100%, 200%, +, the level 164%, a Pick button and ›. A tag at the bottom left reads Frame #5 · image 1 · 9 / 12, and a hint reads Drag to move · scroll to zoom · Esc back.
Keep Enter
Keep the picks and let the run go on.
Step back Esc
Step back a mode: Zoom to Detail, Detail to Grid. From Grid it tucks the picker away; a waiting pill at the bottom of the screen opens it again, picks intact.
Keep all sends everything on. Stop branch stops the nodes after this one; the rest of the run finishes normally. Cancelling the run closes the picker.
A short chime plays when the picker opens, and the tab title starts with ● Pick images while something waits, so you notice from another tab. Turn the chime off with Image Filter sound in Settings; turn on Image Filter desktop notification to also get a system notification while the tab is in the background.

sections.title: Labels, sweep grid and Send to Loop
sections.text:
With a Context Loop, each frame is labelled with its number and the options its sweep pinned (for example #3 · red · pencil). Hover a label to see the frame's seed and prompt. A sweep of two or more wildcards opens in Grid as a table. The bar above it picks which wildcard goes on Rows and which on Columns (⇄ swaps them); any others Split by, one small grid per value. Click a row, column or group name to pick all of it. Layout › Frames switches back to the list.
Figure: A sweep of $time × $medium × $mood as a table: rows and columns, split by $mood. Screenshot of the WP Image Filter picker in Grid mode for a sweep of $time, $medium and $mood, laid out as a table. The bar reads Tile size S M L, Layout Table / Frames, Rows $time, Columns $medium, Split by $mood. Two tables sit side by side, $mood calm (2 of 6 picked) and $mood stormy (1 of 6 picked), each with rows dawn and night and columns oil, watercolor and pencil; the picked cells have a green border and tick.
Send to Loop writes your picks back to the loop: the picked frames' seeds are locked (when the loop overrides seeds) and every other frame is bypassed, so the next run repeats only what you kept.

sections.title: Label each image
sections.text:
Every image has a label, and the labels output sends them in step with images, one per item. By default a label is the frame number (the loop's number with a Context Loop), the options its sweep pinned, then the image number when the frame has several: #3 · red · pencil · 2.
- Rename an image under its tile in Grid, or under its title in Detail. Clear the name to get the default back.
- With Same shape an item holds a frame's picks together, so its label has one line per image.
- Pass all labels images #3 · 2 (no picker, so no option names), and Reuse last picks keeps the names from the last pause.
Figure: Grid with a label under every image: the frame number, the swept option and the image number, and one image renamed. Screenshot of the WP Image Filter picker in Grid mode at tile size L: three loop frames of two images each, headed #1 · oil, #2 · watercolor and #3 · pencil, each with 1 of 2 and a Pick frame button. Under every image is its label: #1 · oil · 1, #1 · oil · 2, then hero shot (an image that was renamed), #2 · watercolor · 2, #3 · pencil · 1 and #3 · pencil · 2. Three images are picked. The footer reads 3 of 6 picked from 3 frames, with Send to Loop, Stop branch, Keep all 6 and Keep 3 picked.

sections.title: Refine before it goes on
sections.text:
In Detail, the side panel edits the frame's positive and negative prompt and paints a mask for the upscaler. Edits travel with the picks; tiles show ✎ for an edited prompt and ◐ for a painted mask.
- An edited prompt replaces the text output. Wire a CLIP into the filter's clip input and the conditioning is re-encoded to match; without one the conditioning stays as it was, and the panel says so.
- With Same shape a frame's picks go on together, so a prompt edit covers the whole frame. With One per image it covers just that image.
- A painted mask goes to the masks output, resized to the image. Images you don't paint keep the incoming mask, or an empty one when nothing is wired in. Once painted, the Mask tab previews it: Over image tints the masked part, Mask only shows it white on black, as the output sends it.
Figure: Detail on frame 3: Pick, Compare and Pick frame at the top, then the Prompt tab with each value marked in its own colour (hovering one says which variable set it) and the negative. The strip below groups the images by frame. Screenshot of the WP Image Filter picker in Detail mode on frame #3, image 1. The picture sits between ‹ and › buttons, with a strip of all 12 images under it. The side panel reads Frame #3 · image 1, 1024 × 1024, seed 41814, 5 / 12, with a Pick button, Compare and Zoom; Values lists $hair silver hair, $place desert and the seed, with Pick whole frame (2); the Prompt box marks silver hair and desert in the prompt; the Negative box reads blurry, extra fingers; Mask has a Paint button.
Figure: How the picks carry over. Diagram titled How the picks carry over: 3 frames of 2 images from a Context Loop; frame 1 image 1 and both frame 2 images are picked, frame 3 none. Rows compare IN with OUT (same shape): images, latent and masks keep only the picked items of frames 1 and 2 (frame 2 gets a PAINTED mask); positive / negative keep 'cond red' and turn 'cond blonde' into 'cond blonde, freckles' marked RE-ENCODED; positive text becomes 'blonde hair, freckles…' marked EDITED. Notes: per-frame items follow their frame, batched ones are sliced; an edited prompt is re-encoded when a CLIP is wired; One per image emits single-image items.

sections.title: Paint a mask
sections.text:
M or Paint on the Mask tab opens the painter over the image. A mask is not just on or off: each pixel can be part-way masked, and inpainting changes those parts less, so soft edges blend in without a seam.
- Brush paints where you drag. Lasso: drag around an area and let go to fill it. Fill: click to fill the area under the pointer, up to the lines you painted (paint an outline, then fill its inside), or click a painted area to take all of it.
- Paint adds to the mask and Erase takes it away, with any tool (X swaps).
