- Size is the brush ([ and ] change it). Hardness softens the edge of the brush, lasso and fill; at 0% the edge fades over half the brush size. Strength masks part-way: one stroke at 50% stays 50% where it crosses itself, and a second stroke adds on top.
- A ring under the mouse is the brush at its real size (dashed when erasing, with a dotted inner ring where a soft edge starts).
- Undo and Redo (Ctrl+Z, Ctrl+Shift+Z) step through strokes, Invert and Clear while the painter is open.
Figure: The painter: a soft brush stroke at the top, an outline filled with Fill, and a soft-edged Lasso on the right. The side panel has the tools, Paint / Erase, Size, Hardness and Strength, then Undo, Redo, Invert and Clear. Screenshot of the WP Image Filter picker in Detail with the mask painter open on frame #1 · oil, image 1. Over the picture, painted in a red tint: a soft brush stroke across the top, a solid oval filled with the Fill tool over the lower left, and a soft-edged lasso shape on the right that fades out. The side panel reads Mask painted with a Done button, then the tool switch Brush / Lasso (selected) / Fill, the switch Paint (selected) / Erase, sliders Size 80 px, Hardness 0% and Strength 100%, buttons Undo, Redo, Invert and Clear, and a hint about hardness and strength.

sections.title: Settings on the node
sections.text:
Figure: WP Image Filter after a run, next to a Preview Image of the three images it kept. Screenshot of a WP Image Filter node after a run, wired into a Preview Image. The node lists its inputs and matching outputs (images, latent, masks, positive, negative, positive_text, negative_text, context, extra_1, extra_2, clip in and picks out). Under When it runs: Mode Pause & pick (Reuse last picks, Pass all), Send picks as Same shape, Timeout 600 s then keep all. The Last run strip reads 3 of 12 kept · frames 1, 5, 10 with three thumbnails, and the Preview Image shows the same three landscapes.
Mode
Pause & pick asks every run. Reuse last picks keeps the same picks without asking, and asks again when they no longer fit. Pass all lets everything through.
Send picks as
Same shape keeps each frame's picks together as one batch. One per image sends every pick as its own item, with its own copy of its frame's prompt, conditioning and Context.
Timeout
Seconds to wait; 0 waits until you answer. After a timeout it keeps all, keeps the first image, or stops the branch.
The Last run strip under the settings shows what the last run kept.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Context Loop WP Prompt Assembler WP Seed List

pages.title: WP Label & Grid
pages.blurb: Put labels on images and lay them out in a labelled grid or XY plot.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Comparing runs side by side is easier when every image says what it is. WP Label & Grid writes a label on each image and, if you like, lays them all out in one grid with row and column headers. It takes whatever a workflow produces: one image, a batch, a list, or a Context Loop's frames of batches.
Good for
- Turning a sweep into an XY plot with headers
- Stamping each image with its frame, seed or settings
- One contact sheet of a whole loop
Better with something else
- Picking images to keep: that is the WP Image Filter

sections.title: Set it up
sections.text:
Figure: Wire the Image Filter's images and labels into the node. The labels name each frame's sweep options, so the grid can sort by them. Steps: WP Context Loop (a sweep) → frames → WP Image Filter (images + labels) → images, labels → WP Label & Grid (labelled grid). Flow diagram of three nodes left to right: WP Context Loop (a sweep), an arrow labelled frames, WP Image Filter (images + labels), an arrow labelled images, labels, and WP Label & Grid (labelled grid). Caption: wire the Image Filter's images and labels into the node; the labels name each frame's sweep options, so the grid can sort by them.
- Wire your images into images. Labels are optional.
- Pick where the label goes in the node's panel.
- Run once. The panel says what came in and marks the grid preset that fits it; click Use it, or pick another preset.
Figure: A 3 × 3 sweep with the XY plot preset: rows from label part 2, columns from label part 3, the cells keep their #N on a see-through band. Screenshot of a canvas with three nodes. On the left, Your images (a 3 × 3 sweep) sends images and labels into WP Label & Grid. Its panel reads 9 images · labelled · grid 1645×2246 at the top; under LABEL the text is {label}, placed below the image with Over image on, the default font at automatic size, white text on a see-through black band; under GRID the switch is on and the XY plot preset is picked from a row of presets (Fit the run, Sheet, Side by side, Frame rows, Frame columns, XY plot, No grid), with Rows from label part 2 (dawn, noon, night), Columns from label part 3 (pastel, vivid, ink) and the title Time of day × style. Its grid output feeds a Preview Image showing a 3 × 3 grid of mountain landscapes under that title, with column headers pastel, vivid, ink, row headers dawn, noon, night, and each cell labelled #1 to #9 on a band over its bottom edge.

sections.title: Ports
sections.text:
images
One image, a batch, a list, or a list of batches (a Context Loop's frames). Required.
labels
Optional text, one entry per item and one line per image of its batch. One line covers the whole batch, and a single one-line label covers every image of every item. The Image Filter's labels output fits straight in. One typed text with a line per image works too.
label_text
Optional text from another node for what each image shows; {label}, {index} and the other tokens still work. A list gives one text per item, the last one covering any item past it.
title
Optional text from another node for the grid title. Once wired, the panel's Title box shows that it comes from the wire.
row_headers, column_headers
Optional text from another node, one header per line (a list gives one header per entry). Wiring one sets that side to typed headers and replaces its dropdown on the panel. Like a built-in widget's, each text input's dot sits beside the field it feeds and shows when you hover that field or wire it.
images (out)
The labelled images, in the shape they came in. A batch stays a batch.
grid (out)
Every image in one labelled grid. The node also shows it on the canvas, so it can end a branch.

sections.title: Labels
sections.text:
Text
What each image shows. {label} is the incoming label (the default), {frame} and {image} count from 1 per input item, {index} counts across all images, {count} is how many there are. \n breaks a line.
Place
Above, below, left or right adds a strip beside the image. Over image draws a see-through band over the top or bottom and keeps the size. The last button draws no label.
Font and size
Your system fonts plus any you drop into the extension's fonts folder; type to search. An empty size is automatic: a share of the image width, so labels read the same at 512 px and at 4K.
Colours
Click a swatch for the colour square and a hex box. The strip or band also has an opacity, and None drops it.
Without a labels input the template still works: #{index} numbers every image.

sections.title: Grid presets
sections.text:
Images can come as one batch, a list, or a list of batches, and each wants a different grid. A preset sets the layout and headers in one click; change anything after.
Fit the run
The default. Follows what comes in: one batch fills a sheet, a few single images sit in one row, a list of batches gets one row per frame.
Sheet
Every image in turn, filled into a near-square sheet, or the columns you set.
Side by side
Every image in one row, for comparing a few runs.
Frame rows / Frame columns
One row (or column) per frame of a loop, its batch across. With the Image Filter's labels they are headed #1, #2, …
XY plot
Rows and columns from the two label parts that vary, each part's values as headers.
No grid
Only label the images.

sections.title: The grid
sections.text:
Layout
Fit the run, one row or column per frame, fill rows (with a column count), all in one row, all in one column. Label-part headers set the layout themselves.
Rows, Columns
No headers, typed (one header per line in the box that opens), or a label part. The list shows what each part held on the last run.
Title, Spacing
A line of text above the grid; the gap between cells, the edge around the grid, and the cell width (empty keeps image sizes, a number scales every cell to it).
Colours
The grid's background and the colour of headers and title. Reset puts spacing and these back.
A label can hold parts joined by · . The Image Filter writes #3 · red · pencil: the frame, then the sweep options in the loop's order, then the image number when a frame has more than one. With Rows from label part 2 and Columns from label part 3 (what the XY plot preset picks here), every image lands under its options whatever order it came in, the options become the headers, and the cells keep just #3. Two images with the same options (another seed) repeat the row.

sections.title: Good to know
sections.text:
- Long labels wrap to the image width; past three lines they end with "…".
- Images of different sizes are centred in the largest cell.
- A font the machine doesn't have (a workflow from someone else) falls back to the default.
- Grids are capped at 16384 px on the longest side. Use the cell width to keep them small.
- Wire grid into a Save Image node to keep it.

pages.title: WP Debug
pages.blurb: See every variable, pick and warning after a run.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
Wire a Context's output into a WP Debug. After each Generate it shows everything that reached that point. It has no output and changes nothing.
Figure: A WP Context with the Starter set bundle and Hair, feeding WP Debug. The Variables tab lists each variable, its value, its tags and which module set it. Screenshot of a WP Context feeding a WP Debug. The Context (seed 42, fixed, modules 7 / 7) has the Starter set bundle expanded (Starter subject, Starter pairing, Starter mood, Starter style, Starter scene, Starter accent) and a Hair wildcard below it. The WP Debug header reads seed 42, 7 steps, clean run, with tabs Variables (6), Trace (7), Warnings and Raw and a Filter variables box. The Variables tab lists $subject cat (feline) and $mood dramatic (intense), both marked hidden from the prompt, then $style oil painting, $scene dramatic cat, $accent cinematic lighting and $hair silver hair (cool), each with the module that set it on the right.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- Seeing why one run came out as it did: every variable, who wrote it, each pick and warning
Better with something else
- How often options come up over many seeds: use the Test Runner

sections.title: The tabs
sections.text:
Variables
Every $variable and its value at this point, with the module that set it. The quickest way to check what your wildcards picked. Negative words show under the value in red, with the module they came from when it isn't the variable's own.
Trace
Every module in the order it ran, grouped by Context. Open one to see why it did what it did: a wildcard's odds and the constraints that changed them, which derivation branch ran, and the negative each one left.
Warnings
What came up during the run, such as missing variables or a constraint that changed nothing. Look here first when something seems off.
Raw
Everything as JSON, with a download button. Handy for bug reports.
The filter box at the top of each tab searches by variable name or warning.

sections.title: Where to put it
sections.text:
After one Context to check that step, or after the last to see everything. Use as many as you like; each shows what it sees at its own spot.
Figure: Two Context → Debug pairs. The second Debug shows a negative ('umbrella') riding along with $weather. Screenshot of two Context → Debug pairs stacked. The top WP Context holds Starter subject and Pose; its Debug lists $subject dog (canine) and $pose standing. The bottom WP Context holds Hair and Weather; its Debug shows a red '1 negative' badge and lists $hair black hair (cool) and $weather light rain with the negative '- umbrella' under it (tag wet). It shows that Debug lists each variable's value, tags and source, and the negative words a pick carries.

sections.text: Conflicts & warnings Warning & conflict types

pages.title: WP Var → Int
pages.blurb: Turn a number in a $variable into a whole-number input.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
A pick can hold a number: a size like 1920x1080, a step count like 30 steps, or just 512. WP Var → Int takes the number out and gives it to any node that wants a whole number. If there's no number, it gives your default.
Figure: WP Var → Int reads $resolution (1024) and sends it to Empty Latent Image's width. Screenshot of a WP Context holding a Render settings fixed value ($resolution, $cfg and one more) wired into a WP Var → Int set to resolution. Its last execute line shows 1024, parsed from '1024', with index 0 and default 0. The value output feeds a Preview as Text that prints 1024 and the width input of an Empty Latent Image. It shows a text variable driving a number input.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- A pick that drives a whole number: $steps, a width or height, a seed
Better with something else
- Text that should stay in the prompt
Hide the variable it reads (the globe on its row), so the value doesn't print in the prompt. The node re-runs only when that value changes.

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
context (in)
The Context that holds the $variable.
var_name
The $variable to read. The list shows every variable the wired Context has.
index
Which number to take when there are several: 0 is the first, 1 the second. Usually 0.
default
The value to use when the variable is missing, has no numbers in it, or the index is beyond what was found. The node never stops the run; it uses this instead.
value (out)
The whole number, for any INT input: width, steps, batch size and so on.

sections.title: How it finds the number
sections.text:
The node finds every whole number in the text (a minus sign counts), in order, and index picks one:
- 1920x1080: index 0 gives 1920, index 1 gives 1080
- 30 steps: index 0 gives 30
- hello: no number, so the default
For width and height from one $resolution, use two WP Var → Int nodes on the same variable: index 0 for width, index 1 for height.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Var → Float WP Var → Bool WP Context

pages.title: WP Var → Float
pages.blurb: Turn a number in a $variable into a decimal input.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
A pick can hold a number such as 0.75, cfg 7.5 or 8. WP Var → Float takes it out and gives it to any node that wants a decimal. Whole numbers work too. If there's no number, it gives your default.
Figure: WP Var → Float reads $cfg (7.5) and sends it to the KSampler's cfg. Screenshot of a WP Context holding a Render settings fixed value wired into a WP Var → Float set to cfg. Its last execute line shows 7.5, parsed from '7.5', with index 0 and default 0.00. The value output feeds a Preview as Text that prints 7.5 and the cfg input of a KSampler. It shows a variable driving a sampler setting.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- A pick that drives a decimal: $cfg, a LoRA strength, a denoise
Better with something else
- Text that should stay in the prompt
Hide the variable it reads (the globe on its row), so the value doesn't print in the prompt. A derivation can write it from another pick (“if $model_family is flux, $cfg is 1”). The node re-runs only when that value changes.

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
context (in)
The Context that holds the $variable.
var_name
The $variable to read. The list shows every variable the wired Context has.
index
Which number to take when there are several: 0 is the first, 1 the second. Usually 0.
default
Used when the variable is missing, has no number, or has fewer numbers than the index. The node never stops the run; it uses this instead.
value (out)
The number, for any FLOAT input: CFG, denoise, a LoRA strength and so on.

sections.title: How it finds the number
sections.text:
The node finds every number in the text, in order, and index picks one:
- cfg 7.5: index 0 gives 7.5
- 1920x1080: index 0 gives 1920.0, index 1 gives 1080.0
- 1.5e-3: index 0 gives 0.0015
- hello: no number, so the default

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Var → Int WP Var → Bool WP Context

pages.title: WP Var → Bool
pages.blurb: Turn a yes/no in a $variable into a true/false input.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
WP Var → Bool reads a $variable as true or false. true, yes, on and 1 are true; false, no, off and 0 are false. Wire it into a switch or toggle, and a wildcard pick decides whether it's on.
Figure: WP Var → Bool reads $hires ('yes') and outputs True. Screenshot of a WP Context holding a Render settings fixed value wired into a WP Var → Bool set to hires. Its last execute line shows True, parsed from 'yes', with index 0 and default false. A Preview as Text node prints True. It shows a word such as yes being read as a true / false value for another node.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- A pick that flips a switch in the graph: $hires into a switch node, a detailer on or off
Better with something else
- Text that should stay in the prompt
Hide the variable it reads (the globe on its row), so the value doesn't print in the prompt. The node re-runs only when that value changes.

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
context (in)
The Context that holds the $variable.
var_name
The $variable to read. The list shows every variable the wired Context has.
index
Which yes/no word to use when there are several: 0 is the first, 1 the second. Other words don't count.
default
Used when the variable is missing or has no yes/no word. The node never stops the run; it uses this instead.
value (out)
True or false, for any BOOLEAN input: a switch node, a toggle and so on.

sections.title: How it reads the text
sections.text:
The node splits the text at spaces, commas, semicolons, pipes and slashes and checks each word (capitals don't matter). Other words are skipped and don't count for the index:
- True: true, yes, on, 1
- False: false, no, off, 0
- Everything else (e.g. maybe, 1.5, hello) is ignored
So true maybe false has two: index 0 is true, index 1 is false.
A wildcard with options on and off through WP Var → Bool switches any true/false input at random. Weights set how often.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Var → Int WP Var → Float WP Context

pages.title: WP Var → Choice
pages.blurb: Send a $variable into a dropdown: checkpoint, sampler, scheduler, VAE, LoRA.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
WP Var → Choice sends a pick into any dropdown: the checkpoint, the sampler, the scheduler, the VAE or a LoRA name. It reads the real list of the dropdown it's wired into and finds the option your text names, so wai nsfw v14 finds illustrious/waiNSFW_v14.safetensors. A wildcard of model names can then pick the model per image, or per frame in a Context Loop.
Figure: WP Var → Choice reads $checkpoint and sends the matching file to Load Checkpoint. Screenshot of a WP Context holding a Checkpoints wildcard wired into a WP Var → Choice set to checkpoint, match loose, fallback empty, if_no_match use fallback. Its last execute line shows the checkpoint file it sent, with 'Matched … loosely.' under it and 'into Load Checkpoint › ckpt_name' with the option count. The choice output feeds the ckpt_name input of a Load Checkpoint node. It shows a wildcard picking the checkpoint.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- A pick that chooses the checkpoint, sampler, scheduler, VAE or LoRA
- Trying several models in one loop: a wildcard of model names, one per frame
Better with something else
- Text that should stay in the prompt
- A number (steps, size): use WP Var → Int or Float
Hide the variable it reads (the globe on its row), so the model name doesn't print in the prompt. Add WP Model Info after the loader and your rules can see which model was picked.

sections.title: Controls
sections.text:
context (in)
The Context that holds the $variable.
var_name
The $variable to read. The list shows every variable the wired Context has.
match
How close the text must be to an option: exact, loose (the default) or closest. See below.
fallback
A dropdown of the options of the input it's wired into, filled when you connect it. Used when nothing matches or the variable is empty. (first option) means the first option in the list.
if_no_match
use fallback carries on with the fallback and warns you. stop the run stops here and lists some of the options.
choice (out)
Wire it into a dropdown input: ckpt_name, sampler_name, scheduler, vae_name, lora_name and so on. The line under the picker names what it feeds and how many options that has.

sections.title: How it matches
sections.text:
- exact: the text must be an option, letter for letter.
- loose: capitals, folders, the file extension, spaces, _, - and . don't matter, so Euler A finds euler_ancestral. If that finds nothing, it takes the shortest option that starts with your text, then one that contains it, so dpmpp 2m finds dpmpp_2m and not dpmpp_2m_sde.
- closest: loose, and then the most similar option, so a typo like dreamshapr still lands.
After a run the picker shows what it sent and how it found it. When it used the fallback, the line turns amber and a warning pops up.
Without this node ComfyUI doesn't check text that comes in through a wire: a name that isn't in the list only fails inside the loader. WP Var → Choice checks it first.
Wired into a switch or another node without a list, the text passes through unchecked and the picker says so.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Model Info WP Context Loop WP Var → Int WP Var → Bool

pages.title: WP Note
pages.blurb: A note that explains a workflow: a step, a tip or a label, with a docs link.

sections.title: What it's for
sections.text:
WP Note explains a workflow on the canvas. It looks like a panel, not a node: no title bar, no frame and no sockets, in the classic renderer and in Nodes 2.0, and its selection outline hugs the panel. It is left out of the prompt; its text is saved with the workflow.
Figure: A Step card with docs buttons, a Warning card with its own icon, a Tip sticky, and a Label showing its hover card. Four WP Notes on the canvas with no node frame around them. A Step 1 card, Load your model, with a $model_family code span and two docs buttons (WP Model Info, Writing prompts for your model); an amber Warning card with a triangle icon and a lock icon in its text; a green Tip sticky with a lightbulb, tinted with its colour; and a small purple Label pill, Label each frame, whose hover card is open above it with the label's text, a The grid docs button and an Edit button.

sections.title: When to use it
sections.text:
Good for
- Numbered steps through a shared workflow
- A warning or tip next to the node it is about, with its docs page one click away
- A small label over a group of nodes
Better with something else
- A heading for a group of nodes: ComfyUI's own group title

sections.title: Looks
sections.text:
Card
A panel with a coloured edge on the left. The title and the text show on the canvas.
Sticky
The same panel, tinted with the colour.
Label
A small pill with the title only, sized to it. Hover it to see its text and links in a card; move onto the card to click them. Marks on the pill show that it has text (lines) or a link (chain).

sections.title: Moving, sizing and editing
sections.text:
Unpin a note to drag it like any node. A Card or Sticky resizes from its corner: the width is yours and the height follows the text. A Label sizes itself to its title. Double-click a note, press its pencil or press Edit on a label's hover card to open the editor; Done goes back to reading.
Tone
Step (a numbered circle), Icon (pick any icon from the list next to it) or Plain (no badge).
Colour
Presets that follow the theme (Accent, Tip, Info, Warning, Danger, Teal, Violet, Neutral), or any colour from the picker.
Look
Card, Sticky or Label (above).
Pinned
ComfyUI's own pin: a pinned note can't be moved or resized by accident. New notes start pinned.
Title
Shown in bold at the top, or on the pill of a Label.
Text
Markdown, with the formatting bar below over it.
Keys you type in the editor stay in the editor: Delete, Ctrl+Z and ComfyUI's other shortcuts don't reach the canvas.

sections.title: The formatting bar
sections.text:
Figure: The editor with the link panel open: a docs page found by typing, one of its sections, and a button with an icon. A WP Note open in its editor next to a finished Step card. The editor has Tone (Step, Icon, Plain) with the step number, Look (Card, Sticky, Label) with the Pinned switch, a row of colour presets with a custom colour field, the Title, and the Text with its formatting bar: bold, italic, strikethrough, code, bulleted and numbered list, quote, link (pressed), icon and a preview eye. The link panel under the bar has Docs page chosen, WP Label & Grid found by typing, its section The grid, the link text, and Button with the Th Large icon, ready to Insert link.
Bold, italic, strikethrough Ctrl+B / Ctrl+I
Wraps the selection in **, * or ~~.
Code
Wraps it in backticks, for a $variable.
Lists and quote
Puts - , 1. or > before each selected line (press again to take it off).
Link Ctrl+K
A Docs page (type to find any page of these docs, then pick a section or the whole page) or a Web address, drawn as a Button with an icon or as a Text link. The selected text becomes the link's text.
Icon
Any PrimeIcons icon, searchable, in a colour or the text's own.
Preview (eye)
Shows the note as it will read.

sections.title: Links and icons in the text
sections.text:
The bar writes these for you; you can also type them. A note can hold any number of links, anywhere in the text. Any other kind of link shows as plain text.
[Read more](https://example.com)
A link that opens in a new tab.
[Seeds](docs:seeds-and-loops)
A link to that page of these docs.
[The grid](docs:wp-label-grid#s-the-grid)
A link to one section of it.
[Start here](docs:quick-start){button pi-play}
The link drawn as a button with an icon. {button} alone has no icon.
:pi-heart: :pi-heart:{#rrggbb}
An icon, optionally in a colour: a hex code like the custom colour field shows.

sections.title: A note that is also a bookmark
sections.text:
Turn on Also a bookmark at the bottom of the editor and the note joins the Bookmarks dock: pick where it lands on screen, its zoom and a shortcut, the same settings as a WP Bookmark, with the same clash check. A new one gets the next free shortcut. The dock shows it with the note's colour and icon, and a small bookmark mark on the note (its tooltip names the key) says it is one.
Figure: A note open in its editor with Also a bookmark on, a note card with its bookmark mark, and the dock listing both next to a WP Bookmark. Screenshot of WP Notes used as bookmarks. On the left, the Bookmarks dock lists three rows: 1 Load your model (a blue bookmark icon, Alt + 1, highlighted after a jump), 2 Sampler (an amber lightning icon, Alt + 3) and 3 Label each frame (a red bookmark icon, Alt + 2). In the middle, the note Label each frame is open in its editor (Step 2, Card, colour #ef4444, its title and Markdown text); at the bottom the Also a bookmark switch is on, with the hint Jump here from the Bookmarks dock or a shortcut, and under it Lands at with the centre of a 3 × 3 grid picked (Centre of the screen, 24 px in), Zoom set to 1 ×, and the shortcut Alt + 2, then Done. On the right, the note card Load your model (step 1, blue) shows a small bookmark mark in its head next to the pencil, and below it a WP Bookmark node, Sampler, in its one-line read view: Centre · 1.25×, Alt + 3, Go and a pencil.
Unlike a WP Bookmark, a note can't be hidden on the canvas (it is there to be read), and muting it turns its shortcut off without fading it.

pages.title: Wildcard
pages.blurb: A list of options; each run picks one into a $variable.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A wildcard holds options such as "a cat", "a dog", "a fox" and picks one each run. The pick goes into a $variable you name, so your template and later modules can use it. Weights make some options more likely, and tags let constraints and filters work with groups of options.
Good for
- Any choice something else reacts to: a constraint, a derivation, Match variable, a sweep
- Any list you want weights, tags, a fallback or Test Runner counts on
- A shared vocabulary with no variable, drawn through @{} references
Better with something else
- Always-on text: use Fixed Values
- A tiny variant inside one option: an inline {a|b}
- A phrase built from other picks: use a Combine
Figure: The Starter subject wildcard: four options with weights, chances and categories, and the Runtime buttons (Lock pick, Hide from prompt, Hold across run, Match variable). Screenshot of the Starter subject wildcard editor opened from a WP Context row (WILDCARD, Library entry · weighted options resolved per pick). Identity shows Display name Starter subject and Variable binding $subject. The Pool section has Pick 1 – 1 and an Advanced button, and a table of four ticked options: cat and tiger (category FELINE) and dog and wolf (category CANINE), each with weight 1 and a 25% probability bar; 4 of 4 enabled. The Runtime row has Lock pick, Hide from prompt (on), Hold across run and Match variable. The footer has Edit library entry in SPA, Reset overrides, Save to library, Cancel and Save.

sections.title: Make one
sections.text:
- In the manager, use Quick create → Wildcard on the dashboard, or the new button on the Wildcards page.
- Give it a name. The variable name follows it ($subject).
- Add options, one per row, or paste a list with Bulk edit.
- Save, then add it to a WP Context with Add module.

sections.title: Option fields
sections.text:
Value
The text that goes into the prompt, such as "a cat". It can hold {a|b} choices and @{} references to other wildcards.
Weight
How likely the option is next to the others: weight 2 comes up twice as often as weight 1. 0 switches it off without deleting it.
Sub-categories (tags)
Labels on an option, such as "feline" or "warm". An option can have several. Constraints and the category filter work with them, and you can sort them into groups (species, temperature).
Null option
An option that prints nothing, for "sometimes leave this out". At most one per wildcard.
Fallback
Hover an option's probability and click "set as fallback". It rolls like any other option, and is also used when nothing else is left to pick (constraints ruled everything out, or every weight is 0). Give it weight 0 if it should only ever stand in. One per wildcard. WP Debug and the Test Runner say "Fallback used" when it kicks in.

sections.title: Change it for one node
sections.text:
Open the row's editor on the node to change how this one use behaves. The library entry stays as it is.
Variable binding
The variable this use writes. It starts as the library's; change it to use the same wildcard twice ($hair and $hair_b) without one overwriting the other.
Option toggles
Untick options this use may not pick. Leaving one ticked fixes the value, though a constraint can still rule it out (keep a fallback for that).
Per-use weights
Change an option's weight for this use only. The library editor doesn't show them.
Category filter
Only pick options with certain tags, e.g. "feline and warm, not lynx" (a comma means or). Click the tag pills or type it under Advanced.
Pick, separator, Allow repeats
Pick several options at once. See below.
Exclude null
Leaves the null option out for this use, so something always prints.
Fallback
Untick the fallback to switch it off for this use; then nothing prints when nothing is left.
Match variable
Instead of rolling, pick the option whose text equals a variable's value (case doesn't matter), e.g. $model_variant from WP Model Info. No match uses the fallback, or rolls as usual. This is how a variable can drive a constraint.
Lock pick
Keeps the same pick on every Generate and loop frame until you unlock it. Good for an art style you've settled on.
Hold across run
The same pick on every frame of one loop run, a new one next Generate. Good for a character who stays the same through a story.
Hide from prompt
The variable prints nothing, but constraints, combines and derivations can still use it.
To fix one value on a node, untick every other option or use Lock pick.

sections.title: Pick several at once
sections.text:
Set Pick to a range, e.g. 2–3, and the wildcard picks that many options, joined by the separator. Allow repeats lets the same option come up twice. $colors prints them all ("red, blue, green"); $colors.0 is just the first ("red").
When picking several, the null option is left out. Set the lower end to 0 for "maybe none".

sections.title: Wildcards inside wildcards
sections.text:
An option can hold a reference to another wildcard: type @ and pick it. Picking "@{color} jeans" then also picks a color. A reference can narrow what it draws, such as only the warm colors. See Chips & references.
Option text can't read a $variable: $mood in an option prints as typed. To build text from other picks, use a Combine.

sections.title: Tags you can read as variables
sections.text:
Each tag group has a kind, set on its header:
classify (default)
The tags describe what the option is: casual, t-shirt, skirt. All of them are true at once, and a constraint on the group uses them together.
accepts
The tags are choices the option offers: an outfit that goes with sneakers, heels or sandals. One of them is rolled with the pick, you can print it as $outfit.SHOES, and a constraint reacts to that one tag.
Ask what the tag says about the option. "Is this outfit casual?" is classify. "Which shoes go with this outfit?" is accepts.
Reading an accepts group
If $outfit has an accepts group named SHOES, then $outfit.SHOES is the shoe rolled with this run's outfit. It is rolled once, so it reads the same everywhere. With several picks, $outfit.0.SHOES is the first pick's. Only accepts groups can be read this way; anything else prints nothing and gets a warning. The group name must be letters, digits and underscores, and renaming it breaks templates that read it.

sections.title: With constraints
sections.text:
A Constraint can change this wildcard's odds based on another pick, such as making "stormy" likelier when the subject is "ocean". It must sit after the source wildcard and before this one.
Figure: Source wildcard, then the constraint, then the target wildcard. The #1 badges link the constraint to its target. Screenshot of a WP Context (modules 3 / 3) wired into a WP Prompt Assembler. The Context rows, top to bottom: Starter subject ('$subject · 4 options'), Starter pairing, a constraint marked #1-all ('$subject → $mood · 2×2'), and Starter mood marked #1 ('$mood · 4 options'). The Assembler's template is 'a $mood $subject, masterpiece' and its preview reads 'a sleepy wolf, masterpiece'. It shows the order: source wildcard, then the constraint, then the target wildcard it changes.
Constraints react to picks, not variables. To steer one from a variable (such as the loaded model), give a wildcard options that spell the variable's values and set Match variable on it. WP Model Info has an example.

pages.title: Import wildcard packs
pages.blurb: Bring in A1111, Forge, Dynamic Prompts, PPP or Impact Pack wildcards.

sections.title: Import a pack
sections.text:
- Open Import / Export → Wildcard packs.
- Choose a folder, files or a .zip, or drop them on the page. It reads .txt lists and .yaml, .yml and .json files. Wildcard folders of extensions installed in ComfyUI (Impact Pack, Dynamic Prompts, Easy-Use, PPP, LoRA Manager) are listed below: click Convert to use one.
- Review the plan: what each list becomes and how well it carries over.
- Pick what to import (everything starts selected) and import.
Importing the same pack again finds the wildcards you already have instead of adding copies.
Figure: A small fantasy pack in review: 49 files become 11 wildcards, 43 lists merged into 5 tagged wildcards. Open here is characters, 11 lists merged into one wildcard; each list shows the tags that pick it, and Keep these lists separate undoes the merge. Screenshot of the wildcard import review page for a pack named fantasy-pack: 11 wildcards with 285 options from 49 files, where 43 lists were merged into 5 tagged wildcards. Tiles count 3 Entry point, 3 Composition, 5 Vocabulary and 0 Group, and a How it carries over bar reads Exact 10, Close 0, Needs a look 1. Domains on the left: All, prompts (with a red dot), characters, scenes and Loose files. The table lists each wildcard with its role, options, used by and carries over; prompts/landscape needs a look. The merged characters wildcard (11 lists) is open: one wildcard made from 11 lists under characters/, with tag groups and its lists such as hair + colors + red and races + elf, and a Keep these lists separate button. On the right are Import settings (pack name, library tag, category, Bundle the entry points, Merge related lists, Apply) and a conversion note that ${name} variables stay as plain text. A Continue to import button sits at the bottom.

sections.title: What you get
sections.text:
- Folders of small lists become one tagged wildcard. hair/colors/red.txt and hair/colors/blonde.txt become one hair/colors wildcard whose options are tagged red and blonde. Untick Merge related lists to keep every list separate.
- Logic becomes stacks. A line that rolls variables, a template reference with arguments or an if-condition becomes a bundle of modules that run together: wildcards that roll each variable once, constraints that keep picks consistent, and a Combine that writes the prompt. Drop it on a Context.
- You see what it makes. Each stack and entry point is rolled a few times on the real engine before you import, and the review shows those prompts.
- References keep working. __name__ becomes an @{} chip pointing at the imported wildcard, and {a|b} choices work as before.
- Everything gets the pack's tag and a category per top folder, so the pack stays together in your library.
Rows marked Needs a look list what changed. An if on something the pack never rolls once is removed (the choice stays), an if inside a {…} choice keeps only its else branch, a variable read inside a {…} choice rolls its own value, and a reference to a list the pack doesn't contain stays as text.

sections.title: The details
sections.text:
How each part of a pack is converted
Lists and their names
Each list is named by its path the way __name__ finds it: animals/cats.txt is animals/cats, and a YAML key clothing: { tops: [...] } is clothing/tops. A list that isn't merged becomes its own wildcard, and its variable is the last part ($cats, $tops).
Merging related lists
With Merge related lists ticked (the default), a folder of small lists becomes one wildcard, like one you'd build by hand: hair/colors/red.txt, hair/colors/blonde.txt and hair/colors/dark.txt become one hair/colors wildcard whose options are tagged red, blonde and dark. Each folder level is a tag group, and lists with the same name in sibling folders share a tag: female/footwear and male/footwear give a gender group (female, male) and a footwear tag, like the axes of a hand-built wildcard. A folder merges when it holds at least two lists and up to 1,000 options over at most three levels; a bigger folder is split into its subfolders. Entry points stay separate, and so does a list that points at another list in the same folder, because a wildcard can't reference itself.
Tables
When the subfolders of a folder repeat the same list names (beings/elf/prompt.txt, beings/orc/prompt.txt, …) each list name becomes one table wildcard, tagged by the folders in between, so the folder becomes a tag group you can filter or steer. The row shows a table chip.
Tag groups
Open a merged row to see its tag groups. Each one is named after the folder level it came from; type a better name and the pack converts again with it.
Keep separate
Merged rows show a lists chip. Open one to see each list with its tag and the tag groups, and click Keep these lists separate to import that folder as one wildcard per list again; Merge again under the settings undoes it. Untick Merge related lists to keep every list separate.
Roles
The review sorts every wildcard by what it does in the pack. Entry points build a prompt from other wildcards and nothing else uses them. Stacks are modules that run together as one bundle. Compositions build on other wildcards and are used by one. Vocabulary is a plain list. Groups are made for globs and folder references. Copies and stack parts are small wildcards the import built for template references and stacks.
Carries over
Each wildcard is marked Exact, Close (same outputs, but a setting or label didn't carry over) or Needs a look (some text no longer renders as it did). Open a row to see why.
Sample rolls
The import rolls each stack and entry point a few times on the real engine. Open a row to see what it makes. A warning from those rolls marks the row Needs a look.
Domains
The top folders (or YAML top keys) of the pack. Pick one to review it on its own. Each wildcard goes in a category named after its domain, unless you type one category for all.
Library tag
Every module gets the library tag, which starts as the pack's name, so the whole pack sits together on the Tags page.
Bundles
Stacks only (the default) makes one bundle per stack and nothing else. Stacks + entry points by folder also puts the entry points into one bundle per domain, inside one pack bundle. None makes no bundles. Lists always stay in the library, where references reach them.
References
__other__ references become @{} chips that point at the imported wildcard. A reference to a list that was merged points at the merged wildcard, filtered by that list's tags, so it still draws from that list only. A glob like __animals/*__, or a parent key like __clothing__ in Impact packs, becomes a group wildcard that picks one of the matching wildcards, weighted by how many options each has. PPP filters such as __colors'warm'__ become a category filter on the chip. A reference to a wildcard from an earlier import of the pack links to the one in your library.
Variables
A line that sets variables and then uses them (Dynamic Prompts ${season=!{winter|summer}}, PPP <ppp:set>) becomes a stack: a wildcard that rolls each variable once, then a Combine that writes the line into a variable. ${x=v} without ! rolls again at each use, as in Dynamic Prompts. Defaults like ${x:dry} become a derivation that fills the variable only when nothing set it. A variable nothing sets is left for you to fill upstream of the stack.
Template arguments
__outfit(season=winter)__ makes a copy of the outfit list with the variable filled in. When several entry points are copies of one template that differ by one value, Fold template copies (on by default) turns them into one wildcard plus a choice that picks the value, with constraints that keep each pair together. Pin the choice to get one of the originals back.
If-conditions
A PPP <ppp:if> that tests a variable the line rolls becomes a constraint: the options behind each branch only show when the condition holds. A test on the model (_is_sdxl, _is_pony, …) becomes a model check stack: put it after a WP Model Info node and it leaves out what the pack rules out for the loaded model. Conditions on anything else are removed, and the choice stays.
Negatives and LoRAs
PPP <ppp:stn>…</ppp:stn> and Umi **text** go to the option's negative, so the Assembler's negative output carries them. PPP <ppp:ext lora …> becomes <lora:name:weight> text.
Umi AI packs
In Umi YAML the key is the prompt and Tags: lists its tags. Tag queries like <[female][casual|--formal]> become a pick from the matching entries, weighted the same way. Yaml Tags.txt names the tag groups. {20%a|b} weights carry over.
Choice syntax
{a|b}, weights like {2::a|b} and multi-pick like {2$$a|b|c} keep working, and so does __2$$name__: it picks two different values of name. Open ranges like {-2$$a|b} get their missing end filled in, samplers like {~a|b} pick at random, and the default separator is a comma.
Weights, labels and fallbacks
Weighted lines (3::text), PPP labels ('summer, casual'::text) and PPP's else choice carry over as option weights, sub-categories and the wildcard's fallback. A line written twice becomes one option with twice the weight, so the odds stay the same.
Comments and encoding
Lines starting with # are skipped and kept as the module's description, as is the # text inside multi-line YAML prompts. Text after a # with a space before it is cut (so C# survives). Files saved as UTF-8 or Windows-1252 both read correctly.

pages.title: Fixed Values
pages.blurb: Set $variables to text you type.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
Fixed Values sets each $variable to the text you typed, every run. Nothing is picked at random unless you write a {a|b|c} choice in the value.
Use it for text that stays the same: a style like "oil painting", quality tags like "8k, masterpiece", or words you always want in the negative. Put it at the top so every module below can read it.
Figure: The Starter style fixed value: $style = oil painting, with a + negative button for negative words. Screenshot of the Starter style fixed value editor opened from a WP Context (FIXED, Library entry · static $var → value pairs). Identity shows Display name Starter style. The Values table has one ticked row: variable $style, value 'oil painting', with a + negative button under the value and an Add new $var for this instance link below; 1 of 1 enabled. The Runtime row has Lock seed, Hide from prompt and Hold across run, and the footer has Edit library entry in SPA, Reset overrides, Save to library, Cancel and Save.
Good for
- Style and quality tags that never change
- A model's required prefix or a standing negative
- A switch you flip by hand
Better with something else
- Real variety: use a Wildcard (it has weights, tags, constraints and Test Runner counts)
- Text built from other picks: use a Combine
Don't let a fixed value and a wildcard write the same variable: whichever runs later wins, without a warning.

sections.title: Row fields
sections.text:
Name
The variable to set: "style" sets $style.
Value
The text. A {a|b|c} choice adds a little variety; other $variables can't be read here (use a Combine).
Enable / disable
Switch a row off without deleting it, such as an optional quality booster.

sections.title: Change it for one node
sections.text:
Value override
Change a row's value, or its negative, on this node only. An empty negative clears it.
Row toggles
Switch rows on or off on this node only.
Lock seed
Keeps any {a|b|c} choice the same on every Generate.
Hold across run
Keeps the choices the same for one loop run, and rolls again next Generate.
Hide from prompt
The variables print nothing; other modules can still read them.
A fixed value can't read $variables other modules set. To build a value from earlier picks, use a Combine.

sections.title: Try it
sections.text: Create a starter Fixed Values module that sets $style to "oil painting". The starter template prints it every run.

pages.title: Combine
pages.blurb: Build a new $variable from text and other variables.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
Write a template such as $style portrait of $subject, $mood lighting. The combine fills in the variables set above it and writes the result to one new variable, such as $shot, for the Assembler or later modules.
You can also sprinkle {a|b|c} inline picks directly inside the template for any on-the-fly variation that doesn't need its own wildcard.
Figure: The Starter scene combine: '$mood $subject' resolves to 'serene cat' and is stored as $scene. The Negative field sends words to the Assembler's negative. Screenshot of the Starter scene combine editor opened from a WP Context (COMBINE, Library entry · template interpolates $vars into output binding). Variable binding is $scene. The template is '$mood $subject', Detected 2 vars lists $mood and $subject, the preview shows the template and Resolved shows 'serene cat'. A Negative field (NEG) says it goes to the Assembler's negative when its template uses $scene, and a note reads stored as $scene. The Runtime row has Lock seed, Hide from prompt and Hold across run.
Good for
- Joining picks into one phrase: “wearing $outfit and $shoes”
- Printing a hidden driver inside a phrase
- Reading an accepts group as text
Better with something else
- Making a pick: a combine isn't a pick, so nothing can constrain it. Use a Wildcard
- Text that depends on a condition: use a Derivation

sections.title: What you type in the template
sections.text:
- $name prints what that variable holds at this point. A module above must set it.
- {a|b|c} picks one part each run, for small variations that don't need a wildcard.
- $$ prints a plain $.
- $name.0, $outfit.SHOES and $name.neg read one pick of a multi-pick, an accepts group, or a variable's negatives.
- @{} references are dropped here: they print nothing and WP Debug notes it. Put a reference in a wildcard option instead.
The variables your template reads show as chips under it. A chip marked missing means no module above sets that variable.

sections.title: Change it for one node
sections.text:
Template override
Change the template on this node only.
Output variable
Write to a different $variable on this node.
Negative override
Change the combine's negative on this node. An empty one clears it.
Lock seed
Keeps the template's {a|b} choices the same on every Generate.
Hold across run
Keeps the result the same for one loop run.
Hide from prompt
The result prints nothing; other modules can still read it.

sections.title: Try it
sections.text: Create a starter Combine that fills $mood $subject into a single $scene variable. It reads the starter subject and mood wildcards, so build those first, or use "Build starter bundle" to get the whole set.

pages.title: Derivation
pages.blurb: If/then rules: when a variable says one thing, change another.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A derivation checks variables that earlier modules set and changes others to match. For example: IF $subject equals "ocean", append ", with crashing waves" to $mood.
Figure: The Starter accent derivation: when $mood is dramatic, $accent becomes cinematic lighting. Screenshot of the Starter accent derivation editor opened from a WP Context (DERIVATION, Library entry · conditional rule-based variable rewrites). Identity shows Display name Starter accent. Under Rules there is one ticked rule, Rule 1: '$mood = dramatic → $accent = cinematic lighting'; the hint says click a rule to expand, grey text is the library and typing in a field overrides it on this node. The Runtime row has Lock seed, Hide from prompt and Hold across run.
Good for
- Text that follows from a pick (“if winter, add a scarf”)
- A pick that only happens sometimes (an action holding @{Accessories:winter})
- A LoRA or injected value replacing a rolled pick
- Story text on $iteration, and negatives that depend on a pick
Better with something else
- Changing the odds of another pick: use a Constraint
- A long lookup from one pick to another: a constraint on a tagged list
- Overwriting a variable a constrained wildcard sets: the pick is thrown away

sections.title: How rules run
sections.text: A derivation can hold several rules, and every rule is checked, top to bottom, even when an earlier one fired. Inside one rule only the first branch that matches runs: IF, then each ELIF, then ELSE. Several small rules are easier to read than one big one.

sections.title: Tests
sections.text:
equals
The value is exactly this text. Capitals count.
contains
The text appears somewhere in the value. Capitals count.
matches
The value fits a regular expression (a text pattern). A broken pattern never matches.
exists
The variable is there at all. A second switch narrows it: any, is empty (there but empty, such as a wildcard that rolled its null option) or has value.
is set / is unset
Is set: there and not empty. Is unset: missing or empty.
NOT
The NOT switch turns any test around: equals becomes not equals, contains does not contain, and so on. Does not contain and does not match need this version or newer.
A test compares with plain text. $variable, @{} and {a|b} written there are not read. To compare two variables, test one and write the other's values as branches. You can test $colors.0, $outfit.SHOES or $hair.neg like any variable.

sections.title: Several tests in one branch
sections.text:
Click + Condition to add another test. The word between them reads AND (all must match); click it to make it OR (any may match). AND groups tighter than OR, the way it reads, and tests joined by AND are drawn in a box so you see what goes together.
+ Group adds a box yourself: IF $time equals "night" AND ($weather equals "rain" OR $weather equals "fog"). Groups nest up to three deep.

sections.title: Actions
sections.text:
Replace
The variable becomes the action text.
Append
Adds the text at the end. Nothing goes in between, so start it with its own comma (", with a scarf").
Prepend
Adds the text at the start. End it with its own comma ("wet, ").
Add to negative
Leaves the variable's text alone and adds the words to its negative, so they go wherever the variable is printed.
Replace negative
Like Add to negative, but the words replace whatever negative the variable had.
Click + And under an action to add another. They run in order, and each sees what the one before wrote: IF $tier equals "warmup", set $pose to $pose_portrait AND add $pose_portrait.neg to its negative.
An action's text can hold $variables, a {a|b} choice or a @{} reference with a filter, so a rule can pull a fresh pick: cinematic lighting, @{Lighting:dramatic} writes "cinematic lighting," plus a pick from the dramatic lights.
What happens to negatives
Replace swaps the variable's negative for those of the variables its new text read; Append and Prepend keep the old one and add. A reference inside Add to negative never changes a pick.

sections.title: LoRA by model
sections.text: LoRA by model in the editor adds a ready-made rule for WP Model Info: if $model_variant is pony, $loras gets a Pony LoRA tag; if illustrious, an Illustrious one; otherwise nothing. Put your LoRA names in, add a branch per model you use, and write $loras in your template.

sections.title: Change it for one node
sections.text:
Switch off a rule or branch
Skip one rule, or one IF, ELIF or ELSE, on this node only.
Change a value
Change what an action writes, or the text a test compares with, on this node only.
Rule order
Reorder the rules on this node.
Lock seed
Keeps the {a|b} and @{} rolls inside the actions the same on every Generate.
Hold across run
Keeps those rolls the same for one loop run. The tests still run every frame, so a frame can still take another branch.
Hide from prompt
The variables the rules set print nothing; other modules can still read them.

sections.title: Try it
sections.text: Create a starter derivation that sets $accent from the mood: if $mood is "dramatic" it writes "cinematic lighting", otherwise "soft lighting".

pages.title: Constraint
pages.blurb: Let one pick change the odds of another.

sections.title: What it does
sections.text:
A constraint watches the pick of a source wildcard and changes the odds of a target wildcard below it, before the target rolls. The target still picks at random; you're only shifting the odds.
Example: when $weather picks "stormy", boost "dramatic" and "moody" in $mood and reduce "sunny" and "cheerful".
Figure: The Starter pairing constraint: feline subjects lean intense, canine subjects lean calm. Below are exceptions and the target reach (First, Next N, All, Pick). Screenshot of the Starter pairing constraint editor opened from a WP Context (CONSTRAINT, Library entry · source pick → modifies target option weights). The Rule matrix has source Starter subject and target Starter mood; rows feline and canine cross columns calm and intense: feline × calm ×0.3, feline × intense ×3.0, canine × calm ×3.0, canine × intense ×0.3, with a Legend button. Exceptions is empty with an Add extra exception button. Target reach has First, Next N, All (selected) and Pick, with the note 're-weights all 1 downstream target'.
Good for
- Two picks that must agree (winter rules out summer clothes)
- Whole families of options with the tag matrix, single pairs with exceptions
- Allow-lists with Only
Better with something else
- Adding text: use a Derivation
- A narrowing that never changes: a category filter or @{X:tag}

sections.title: Make one
sections.text:
- Create a constraint and pick the Source wildcard (the one that decides) and the Target wildcard (the one that follows).
- In the Rule matrix, set a rule for whole tag pairs: rows are the source's tags, columns the target's. For example, winter × summer clothes = Exclude.
- Add Exceptions for single option pairs. An exception wins over the matrix.
- Check the Preview, save, and add the constraint to your WP Context between the two wildcards.
Figure: Order in the stack: source, then constraint, then target. Steps: Source wildcard (its pick) → if it lands on x → Constraint (reweights) → limits → Target wildcard (picks to match). Flow diagram of three stages left to right: Source wildcard (its pick), an arrow labelled if it lands on X, Constraint (reweights), an arrow labelled limits, and Target wildcard (picks to match). Caption: the constraint nudges the odds of its downstream target instances, every match by default or a narrower set you choose, and it sets no $vars itself.
Order matters: the source sits above the constraint, and the target below it. The source must be a wildcard in the stack; a pick made only inside a reference sets no variable, so a constraint on it never applies.

sections.title: Rule modes
sections.text:
Neutral
No rule. The pair rolls as if the constraint weren't there.
Boost
Makes the target options more likely, by the factor you set.
Reduce
Makes them less likely, without removing them.
Exclude
Removes them from the pool for this source pick.
Only
Makes the row a guest list. When the source picks this, the target can only pick options this row says something about: the ones set to Only, plus any you boosted or reduced (they keep those odds). Everything the row doesn't mention is off, including options you add later.

sections.title: Linking picks with Only
sections.text:
Only ties one wildcard's pick to another's. Add an exception maid → frilled apron in Only mode, and whenever the source picks "maid" the target can only pick "frilled apron". You don't list every outfit to rule out.
- Several Only exceptions for the same source value make a short list: "maid" can pick "frilled apron" or "kimono" and nothing else.
- In the matrix, Only works on tags: summer → open means a summer pick can only reach targets tagged open. The rest of that row shows a faint × so you can see what's shut out. A Neutral cell doesn't count as a rule.
- Boost and Reduce in the same row stay on the guest list with their odds. Formal → Only heels, Boost loafers ×2: a formal outfit gets heels or loafers (loafers twice as often), never sneakers or boots.
- Other source values are unaffected: a "biker" pick still rolls every outfit.

sections.title: Preview
sections.text: The Preview card shows the constraint in numbers: one row per source option, one column per target option, and in each cell the chance of that target option when the source picked that row. A dash means ruled out. A row marked nothing left would leave the target empty, and fallback means the target's fallback option stands in. Other constraints, filters and toggles aren't included.

sections.title: When it rules out everything
sections.text: If, for some source value, every target option is excluded or shut out, the target would come out empty. The constraint row then shows a rules out all badge before you run; hover it to see which source values do it. Allow an option for those values, or mark one of the target's options as its fallback.

sections.title: A missing source or target
sections.text: If the constraint's source or target isn't in your library (you installed it without its wildcards, or deleted one), the editor shows the missing wildcard's name and locks the matrix. Reattach points it at a wildcard you have, or Download from community fetches the missing one. The rules are then mapped onto the new wildcard's tags; rules for tags it doesn't have are dropped, and the editor shows how many first.

sections.title: Try it
sections.text: Create a starter constraint: feline subjects lean intense, canine subjects lean calm. It also creates the two wildcards it needs ($subject and $mood) if you don't have them yet.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text:
Several constraints on one target, reaching only some uses of a wildcard, tag axes and wildcards used inside references: see Constraints in depth.
Constraints in depth Wildcard WP Context

pages.title: Bundles
pages.blurb: Several modules saved together, added in one go.

sections.title: What a bundle is
sections.text:
A bundle is a saved group of modules: a character, a wardrobe, a whole pack. Drop it into a WP Context and all its modules arrive at once, in order. In the stack it shows as one frame you can collapse to keep long setups tidy.
When the pipeline runs, a bundle's modules run exactly as if they sat in the stack on their own. The bundle itself adds nothing; it only groups.
Figure: A WP Context with the Starter set bundle expanded and a loose Pose module below it. Screenshot of a WP Context (seed 42, modules 7 / 7) wired into a WP Prompt Assembler. The Context holds the Starter set bundle (6 mods), expanded inside a frame: Starter subject, Starter pairing, Starter mood, Starter style, Starter scene and Starter accent. Below the bundle is a loose Pose wildcard. The Assembler's template is '$scene, $pose, $style, $accent' with 4 upstream chips, and the preview reads 'sleepy wolf, standing, oil painting, soft lighting'.
Good for
- A set of modules you reuse together: a character, a wardrobe, a whole pack
- Sub-bundles for the sections of a pack
Better with something else
- Keeping two copies apart: a bundle doesn't scope its variables. Insert it twice and rename the second copy's variables

sections.title: Make a bundle
sections.text:
- On the canvas, select rows in a WP Context, right-click and choose Save as bundle.
- In the manager, create one on the Bundles page and add modules to it.
- Drop a saved bundle into a Context with Add Bundle.

sections.title: When you edit a module later
sections.text:
A bundle keeps its own copy of each module. What happens when you edit the original:
- Bundles in the library follow. Saving a module updates it in every library bundle that holds it, and each bundle keeps its own settings for it.
- Bundles already on a canvas don't change by themselves. Their header shows library updated. Right-click the bundle and choose Reset to library snapshot, or Refresh from library on one row, to pull the change.
- Push to library… goes the other way: it saves your canvas edits into the library.
If a module is deleted from the library, the bundle keeps working from its copy, and the row shows a MISSING badge. When you delete a wildcard, the manager lists the bundles that hold it and offers to clean up its other uses.

sections.title: Two copies of one bundle
sections.text:
Inserting a bundle twice gives two independent sets of rows, still linked to the library, and references and constraints inside it keep working. But both copies write the same $variables, and the later one wins. To keep both, rename the second copy's variables (each row's Variable binding), or use Duplicate on single rows, which renames for you ($hair becomes $hair_2).
Extract to library in the bundle editor makes the modules into new stand-alone library modules (a copy you can change freely), points the references between them at the new copies, and leaves the per-use settings behind.

sections.title: Switch a bundle off
sections.text: Each bundle has an enable toggle. Turning it off silences all its modules without touching their own settings; turn it back on and everything is as it was. Handy for testing.

sections.title: Try it
sections.text: Build the whole starter set in one click: the subject, mood, style, scene, accent and pairing modules, plus a bundle that groups them, ready to drop into a Context. Anything you already created from the other pages is reused.

sections.title: Works with
sections.text: WP Context Recommended pack structure

pages.title: Templates
pages.blurb: Save an Assembler template and load it anywhere.

sections.title: What a template is
sections.text:
A template is the text you write in the WP Prompt Assembler: words and $variables, such as $scene, $style, $accent, masterpiece, highly detailed. The Assembler fills in each variable every run.
Saved templates live in your library next to modules, but they don't go on a Context. A bundle reuses a set of modules; a template reuses the wording around their variables.
Good for
- A prompt skeleton you reuse, one per model family (tags or prose)
- A fixed system prompt a model needs
Better with something else
- Variety: a template rolls nothing, and {a|b} prints as typed in the Assembler. Put choices in wildcards
See Writing prompts for your model for the order each model family wants.

sections.title: How it pairs with the Assembler
sections.text:
The Assembler's toolbar has Save and Load. Save puts its template in your library; Load replaces the template with one from the library.
A variable in the template needs a module before the Assembler that sets it. If none does, it prints nothing and is underlined in the preview; add the module or fix the name.

sections.title: Try it
sections.text: Create the starter template, $scene, $style, $accent, masterpiece, highly detailed. Load it into a WP Prompt Assembler and the starter modules fill it in.

pages.title: Warning & conflict types
pages.blurb: Every warning, what it means and what to do.

sections.title: As you build (canvas)
sections.text:
These show on the nodes while you build:
What it flags | Severity | What it means
Shadowed variable | Info | An earlier Context already sets this variable, and this one replaces it. Normal when chaining; shown so you know.
Duplicate variable | Warning | Two modules on the same Context set the same variable; the lower one wins.
Missing variable in template | Warning | The Assembler template uses a $variable nothing before it sets (or one that is hidden).
Constraint source not found | Warning | A constraint points at a source wildcard that isn't in your library.
Constraint target not found | Warning | A constraint points at a target wildcard that isn't in your library.
Constraint source not upstream | Warning | The source wildcard isn't above the constraint, so there's no pick for it to react to.
Constraint target not downstream | Warning | The target wildcard isn't below the constraint (or the constraint's reach covers none of its uses), so it can't change anything.
Rules out all (no fallback) | Warning | For some source picks, every option of the target is ruled out and there's no fallback, so it would print nothing. The hover message names those picks. Allow at least one option for them, or set a fallback.
Injector binding unmatched | Warning | A WP Context Injector row names a variable that nothing before it sets.
Unknown tag group | Warning | A $name.GROUP read names a group that isn't an accepts group on that wildcard, so it prints nothing. Make the tag group accepts, or fix the name.
Option missing an accepts tag | Info | Some options have no tag from an accepts group, so $name.GROUP is empty when they're picked. Tag them, or leave it if empty is fine.

sections.title: After a run (WP Debug → Warnings)
sections.text:
These show up once you run. The labels match what WP Debug shows.
What it flags | Severity | What it means
Unknown variable | Warning | A template or combine used a $variable nothing set, so it printed nothing.
Reference not found | Warning | An @{…} reference points at a wildcard that wasn't found on the node or in the library.
Filter matched no options | Warning | A reference's tag filter left no options, so it printed nothing.
Reference not allowed here | Warning | An @{…} reference sits somewhere that can't use one, such as a combine or the Assembler, so it printed nothing.
Variable not allowed here | Warning | A $variable was written somewhere that can't read one, such as a wildcard option. It printed as typed.
Unknown tag axis | Warning | A $name.GROUP read names a group that isn't an accepts group on that wildcard, so it printed nothing.
Pick has no tag on this axis | Info | The picked option has no tag from the accepts group being read, so $name.GROUP printed nothing.
References nested too deep | Warning | References inside references went too many levels deep, so the deepest ones were left out.
Reference cycle | Warning | References pointed back at each other in a circle; the circle was cut so the run could finish.
Constraint never applied | Info | The constraint's target never ran after it (or wasn't drawn this run), so it changed nothing.
Constraint partial reach | Info | A constraint set to reach the next N (or picked) uses of its target found fewer than that.
Constraint source missing | Warning | The constraint's source wildcard hadn't run yet when the constraint was reached.
Constraint excluded every option | Warning | The constraint ruled out every option of the target and there was no fallback, so it printed nothing.
Fallback used | Info | Nothing was left to pick, so the wildcard's fallback option stood in.
No option matches the variable | Info | A wildcard set to Match variable found no option equal to the variable's value and has no fallback, so it rolled as usual.
Pinned option missing | Warning | A sweep frame (or other pin) points at an option the wildcard no longer has, so that frame rolled instead.
Constraint factor ignored (allow) | Info | A rule set to Allow also has a number; Allow ignores it.
Unknown constraint mode | Warning | A constraint rule has a mode this version doesn't know (probably from a newer pack), so the rule was skipped.
Fixed-values overrides malformed | Warning | The node-only changes on a Fixed Values row couldn't be read, so the library values were used.
Constraint failed to register | Warning | A constraint couldn't be set up, usually because its data is damaged. It was skipped.
Module failed | Warning | A module hit an error and was skipped. The message says which.
Invalid injector name | Warning | A WP Context Injector row used a variable name that isn't valid.
Reserved injector name | Warning | A WP Context Injector row name starts with two underscores, which are kept for the engine.
